I should like to ask the minister a question under this section. I am not in favour of the present system of financing this particular road and its subsidiaries and other affiliations, aided by many bills passed during this war, and even during this session. In view of the vast earnings which this system is making on land, on the sea and in the air, would it not be possible to pay out of income some of these expenditures which are charged up to capital? In the ordinary public ownership ventures, such as the cheap power furnished in Ontario, many of the improvements are charged to income, and come directly from it. If this railway is to operate at cost, and if it is to run on a commercial basis, well and good. But I can tell the house that these two principles are not being carried out at the present time. Why are many of these expenditures for improvements not paid for out of income? Why is it all charged up to capital with heavy refunding charges? I find it difficult to read the auditor's report, and I cannot get this information from the various pamphlets and booklets that are given an ordinary member of parliament. I cannot find any connection between the owership of this railway, which is a public venture, and the principles I have mentioned. If it is going to be a public ownership venture, then let it be a real public
C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities

ownership venture, with the operational costs of the road placed on a commercial basis and the road run from the commercial aspect.
When we look at the cheap light and power in Ontario, a venture which has been a great success, we see the way they meet many betterments and some capital expenditures out of income. What is done in connection with this railway makes but a sorry comparison, loaded up as it is with all sorts of ventures which should never have been entered into. I refer to subsidiaries in the United States, and other capital outlays that never should have been made. Then there is the steamship line running to Port Dalhousie, and many other subsidiary ventures. They are all mixed up together. This system of expenditures and finance bears heavily upon the taxpayers, but they will have to pay for it. We are all wrong in such financing, and it seems to me the system of financing should be overhauled from top to bottom, and in the years to come we should have some way of meeting many of these expenditures out of income instead of charging them up to capital and having them refunded from' year to year. Throughout the country the government has certain properties on which it intends or at one time did intend to erect a public building. Lately I have heard that War Assets Corporation is selling some of these lands. Is that true?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: No. At certain times when we have lands that we do not foresee any use for we have them declared surplus and transferred to War Assets, but speaking from memory I cannot recall one specific case. Before War Assets Corporation was set up, when we had surplus lands, we dealt directly with people and asked for tenders for these lands, but there have been very few cases in the last few years. I cannot at the moment recall a specific instance.
I do not think War Assets Corporation should have the selling of any of the lands of the government, because if they sell them as they have sold other things, God help the people of Canada.
My hon, friend will admit that that is a matter of opinion.
It is not only my opinion but that of a great number of people across the country. I know that people have written in to me asking about certain lands.
If my hon. friend will give me a case I will get all the information I can about it.
I will do that, because I do hope that War Assets is not selling these government lands. I do hope that any such lands that are sold will be sold by tender and not by War Assets.

Would the minister make a statement regarding his plans for the future? Has he a five-year or a four-year plan? What amount cff construction can be expected under the department in the immediate post-war years?

Supply-Public Works

The present
estimates were drawn up in December, 1944, and January, 1945. It will be recalled that at the last session of the last parliament we had the same estimates brought back before us. At that time we were right in the war, although of course preparing for the post-war period. These estimates do not. deal with any post-war projects. They are the regular estimates of the department for the maintenance and repair of the public works we have, and even then not to the full extent required. Hon. members will recall that during the war years the estimates of the department were kept down to the lowest level. In the next fiscal year we shall have to attend to the repairing of nearly every building we have in Canada, because they have been neglected to a certain extent, and my recommendation to the government is for increased amounts in the next estimates so that government property all over the country can be maintained in a good state of repair. Many requests have come from every part of Canada for new buildings, wharves, breakwaters, and all kinds of public works coming under this department. We have our architects and engineers making surveys all over the country, and we have been receiving requests from all over the country. I could not mention any specific cases now; I can only say that they are under consideration and that at the next session I hope to have an increased amount of money to spend on public works throughout the country.

Is -the staff of the
department back to pre-war levels, or is it being increased? I imagine that on paper at least a good deal of work is being done in preparation for the next few years, and it seems to me that a fairly large staff would be necessary even now to do this preliminary work.	.

The number on the staff is perhaps a little lower than it was before the war, or at about the same level, but we are trying to get the services of a good many engineers and architects on a temporary basis. We are having a little trouble in getting qualified technical men because they are not so much interested now in becoming civil servants because of the openings in private enterprise. But we are taking on engineers and architects every month, or trying to get them, to help the regular staff prepare the plans for next year.

I can understand the position of the minister in connection with these estimates. The greater part of the money to ' be voted has already been spent and all that
remains is to finish up the year's business. I would ask him to enlarge a little upon the statement he has just made. Throughout the country from coast to coast the government's public buildings have been perhaps not neglected but allowed to take second place in the plans of the ministry. It would help us to get the full picture if the minister would go on to tell us, though not in detail, of the plans he has for next year and subsequent years. These estimates really deal with something that is past; we are interested also in the future.

I believe requests are coming in from nearly every riding in the country for further repairs to buildings or for the erection of new public buildings. I cannot give details with regard to this town or that city in which it is requested that a building be put up. Most of our buildings are for post office and customs and for other departments. We have to get requests from those department, because they are the ones who must justify the putting up of buildings. The intention is to come back to pre-war conditions in public works and make the necessary expenditures so that our public works shall be in as good condition to serve the public as they were before the war.
Will the minister give the number of employees who have been taken on in his department since June 11, 1945, and the names of those employees?

That is a large order. We have in the department a little over 5,000 employees who are permanent, temporary or seasonal. In the fall we take on a good many firemen for the different buildings, and these would1 have come on since June 11. I am trying to -see what the bon. member is looking for. There has not been any large increase in public buildings since the elections; I did not have the money to pay for them. I am limited by my estimates. Personally I should like to see more employees in the department, but I have not the funds. If the 'hon. member will read these estimates through he will see that they compare with the war years. There is only a difference of some $276 thousand as compared with 1944-45. There may be some extra employees, but I cannot give them from memory.

I would ask the minister to prepare a statement showing the number of employees taken on since June 11 in his department, and giving the names of those employees. That is not a large order. In the minister's own words, he has not expanded) a
Supply-Public Works

great deal. The order is therefore not a large one for any well-run department and I would like to get that information.
We will get these names and the dates of appointments. Most of these appointments are made to replace employees retiring or dying-
That is all I want, sir.
-and the civil service makes the appointments, except for temporary works or in the case of prevailing-rate employees. I will have the information prepared.
Thank you.

Does the department intend to provide better buildings for civil service staff after the war is over? I have in mind some of the old wrecks of buildings that are being used by different departments. Is it the intention to use some of the temporary buildings, which seem to be much better than some of those at present occupied? Or is it the intention to sell the old buildings? One of the buildings I have in mind particularly, is the old horse-stable on Green island which houses the bureau of statistics. These people are dealing mainly with figures all the time, and it is important that they should have proper accommodation. Judging from the outside of the building, I do not think there is any ventilation system. It should have been done away with years ago. The same may be said of many other buildings that are being used by government departments. A few days ago I heard that provision is being made to clear down that old horse-stable and put up another building to house the staff there.

On Green island we have part of the film board staff and the statistical branch of trade and commerce. We are actually preparing plans for the erection of a new film board building. As to the site, we are waiting for a report from Mr. Greber, who is planning the national capital, and the moment we have a site that will fit into the plan for a special kind of film board building we shall be ready to put up that building and clear out the buildings on Green island.

I would ask the minister the same type of question I asked the Minister of Agriculture yesterday. I do not think it is fair to compare the estimate of the previous year with the estimate this year. I would ask him to give, on each vote as the votes appear on page 33, the actual amount that was spent during the particular year. Referring to item 247, which we are now
TMr. Ferguson.]
considering, the minister asked for $191,595 in 1944-45; I should like to know how much he actually spent in that fiscal year. Will the minister from time to time, as he comes to the various items and without having to be asked for the information, give the amount actually spent in connection with each vote? Take number 247.

On vote 247 the estimate in 1944-45 was $191,595; the actual expenditures were $185,989.50. The actual estimate for 1945-46 is $196,195, an increase of $4,600 over the preceding year. This increase comprises: statutory increases $1,065; cost of living bonus, $1,300; travelling expenses, $1,500; miscellaneous adjustments, $735; making the difference of $4,600.

The picture as it presents itself now is entirely different from that shown in the estimates. Of the $191,000, $185,000 is the amount actually spent. We are now asking for $196,000 and instead of an increase of $4,000 roughly the increase is $11,000. I should like to get the same picture in connection with each of these estimate from beginning to end.
I will have that done.
Am I not correct in that?

The hon. member is right. The estimate sometimes is not all expended during the year. It will be found that we have revotes of amounts voted in the preceding year. There is a difference of about eight or nine thousand dollars between the amount voted in 1944-45 and the amount expended. That can be easily accounted for by saying that somebody in the personnel retired and was not immediately replaced.' The salary during that lapsed period would not be paid. Or certain works may have been undertaken and were not completed; therefore the amount was not paid. I believe there is a justification for every case of the kind we have in the estimates.

I am not quarrelling with that at all. I realize that there is justification for anything that is not spent or an amount that may be overspent. But it is totally unfair to compare an estimate of one year with an estimate of the next year, because of the fact that an estimate may be inflated to a very large degree. In this case it is inflated to the extent of $11,000.

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the situation as it exists on some of the lakes in Kootenay West.

Supply-Public Works
The minister will realize that for some years there has been a restricted programme of expenditures in that district. I am not criticizing that so far as the past is concerned, but I do wish to bring to his attention the fact that on the lakes many people are in isolated places without roads and are dependent upon water transportation. I urge upon the minister that in the future he give these people every consideration by providing wharf facilities where it is pos'sible or convenient so to do.
Then there is the question of dredging. In recent years the dredging programme has been restricted until now navigation is difficult between the upper and lower Arrow lakes. Steamers going through there at low water almost touch bottom; in fact they have to be very careful when coming into the low water area. Navigation into the northern end of the lake, where the Columbia enters the Arrow lake, is extremely difficult. I would ask that the minister have the whole matter investigated and these conditions corrected.
May I now say a word with reference to the question of the removal of snags. Years ago the department periodically reihoved snags from the low water areas and close to the docking points so that navigation was reasonably safe at night. I would ask the minister to have the question of the removal of snags on the upper and lower Arrow lakes investigated. There is one other matter, the question of erosion, which has been a constant problem to the Department of Public Works. I refer particularly to the channel between the two lakes. Because the work has not been done in recent years, erosion has taken place in certain areas, I would ask the minister to give that consideration.

I understand the position ur there in Kootenay. We have the snagboat, and we have this dredge, the Samson. The hon. member will find these items mentioned in the estimates. We do a great deal along that line. The intention of the department is to undertake this work in the next year and complete the work which has not been completed in the past.
The hon. member made one request for British Columbia which I received from all parts of the country. I cannot give any other answer than to say that during the war years, and because of the war effort, we did not .receive, and we did not ask parliament for, larger votes.

I should like to pursue a little
further the general administration as it affects the staff, and inquire is to the general policy.
I understood the minister to say when he replied to the hon. member for Simcoe North, that those who were taken on in his department were largely replacements. Is the policy of the department one of promotions? Does the department advertise open competitions? Perhaps I may give a specific instance. I understand that one of the senior officials of his department has about reached the retirement age. How would his position be filled? Would ,it be by competition or promotion?

When there is a vacancy in my department, as in other departments, we send in a request to the civil service commission. They advertise. If it is a senior position, it goes by promotion. It is advertised in the department; a board examines the qualifications, service, seniority, and so forth, and we take on the man who is appointed by the civil service commission.

I think the minister knows- if he does not, his departmental officials do- that for some years I have discussed with his department the matter of repairs to the wharf at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, and a breakwater at Port Morien. The reason I have pursued these two problems year after year is that in the Mqrien case it directly affects the livelihood of a village of about twelve or fifteen hundred people. It is the only industry on that coast. I was assured by both Public Works and Reconstruction that the breakwater at Morien was a post-war project and would be proceeded with in the post-war period. I notice that the estimates make no mention of it, and certainly there is no item in Reconstruction that anticipates anything being done as far as the breakwater there is concerned.
Glace Bay harbour is a very important one, because the sword-fishing industry is largely concentrated there. For the last six or eight months I have wired and written both Fisheries and Public Works with regard to the condition of that harbour. Vote 283, which deals with that matter, makes no mention of that harbour or of any appropriation in regard to it. Neither is there any mention of it in the war estimates or civil estimates of Reconstruction. I think that the least the people affected in both these communities could expect is a definite answer that something is going to be done. We should like to know if anything is anticipated. These people have a right to know so that they can make their arrangements accordingly. I was convinced last year that the matter was left in abeyance pending the termination of the war, but that in the immediate post-war period the Glace Bay harbour and MorieD breakwater would
Supply-Public Works

be major projects for that area, and that things were going to be done. I cannot find any item anywhere which indicates that the government intends to do anything with respect to these two points. The story is well known to Public Works; I am not going to elaborate it, but I should like to know from the minister whether he has anything in mind.

When I first
spoke to the committee I explained that those estimates were prepared in December 1944 and January 1945. We were then right in the midst of the war. The war concluded in May and August, but we still have those same estimates before the house, and as an hon. member remarked, we have spent most of this money, because five-twelfths were voted at one time and one-sixth or two-twelfths at another time. These are estimates which are prepared as I am preparing actual estimates which will be presented at the ensuing session. We prepare them in November, December and January. Now, I would not want to undertake at this time, a discussion of those two projects, Glace Bay harbour and the Port Morien breakwater, but we are having reports prepared by our engineers. I do not think that the hon. member would ask me on these estimates for a definite statement as to the intentions of the department in respect of the new estimates which will come up in February or March of next year, but he may be sure that we are studying and considering those post-war projects. They are post-war projects; do not ask me on these present estimates, which were prepared before the end of the war, for any post-war works. I do not think I could give an answer which would satisfy the hon. member.

I appreciate the minister's
difficulty. If he carries on the same system year after year he is going to be in the same position in 1949. It is not the fault of the people affected that the estimates are handled in that way. You are running on to the end of 1945 with these estimates, and as far as these communities are concerned they can anticipate nothing by the end of 1945. Remember, you have two industries tied up there, with the means of livelihood for the communities. While you prepared those estimates last August, do not forget that the members of this house were sitting at home for three or four months when they could have been here doing business and dealing with these estimates. It is not our fault that we were away. The condition at these two points is serious. I could mention a dozen more cases, but I do not think there is the same urgency in respect of them as there is in [Mr. Gillis.l
these two particular matters, where action is badly needed and should be taken now. The Minister of Reconstruction, who is handling post-war projects, has prepared his reconstruction estimates, and there is not an item in them dealing with these matters. Evidently they are forgotten, so far as those who can sit down and write the necessary appropriations into the estimates are concerned.
We leave here in December. My message to these two sections of the country where there is an urgent problem is, "Nothing is to be done for 1945." We shall come back here next summer, and, you say, the money available under these estimates is all spent. You will start preparing the next estimates in December or January, and by the time they pass through the house all the money will1- again-be spent and there still will not be any appropriation.
That is not the way at all.

That is exactly the way you put it just now. As I said before, I am not concerned about money for projects such as new buildings; I realize that one can get around to those thipgs any time. But where the means of livelihood is directly affected the situation is different. Your department should not have to begin now to study the Glace Bay harbour or the Port Morien breakwater, because you have been dealing with it for the last ten years, throwing a few planks around.
Then you have not been convincing in the past.	.
I was not here except during the war, and you always have the alibi, "There is a war on."

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must protest against a procedure which is growing up, and regarding which my own colleagues are as reprehensible as anybody else, of hon. members speaking across the floor to each other. Every question should be addressed to the committee through the Chair. [DOT]

That is quite true, but I cannot very well blame the present chairman of this committee for the inactivity of the Department of Transport; and while I realize it may not be exactly in order, it is natural,
I think, to talk to the person concerned.
Does the hon. gentleman mean the Department of Transport?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Minister of Veterans Affairs is correct. The procedure, as we all know, is to address all questions to the chairman, and all remarks which are delivered

Supply-Public Works
by any member of the committee should be addressed to the chairman. I agree with what the Minister of Veterans Affairs has said, that sometimes his own colleagues are just as guilty in this respect as are other members of the committee.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I realize that, so I am going to talk direct to you now, and through you to the minister. Mr. Chairman, what I was endeavouring to do was to point out to the minister that despite the fact that for the past six years certain definite commitments have been made verbally to people in the community I represent in this House of Commons, with regard to certain improvements to harbour and breakwater facilities which direcfly affect the means of livelihood of a large number of people, I am rather disappointed, in looking over the public works department estimates, that, regardless of all these promises that in the post-war period these necessary improvements would be undertaken, there is no item in the estimates providing the money to bring about the necessary improvements. Secondly, in checking over the reconstruction estimates for the immediate post-war period, as these were supposed to be post-war projects, I still find not an item there to provide the necessary funds. I should like to find out through you, Mr. Chairman, if the people of the communities affected can expect any relief in the immediate future in the very urgent matter of improving their means of livelihood, as regards repairs to the harbour in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, and the breakwater at Port Morien. I should like to be able to go home and tell the people of these two communities that the alibi offered by the government through the war years, namely that they were fighting a war, concentrating upon that, and spending all their money on it, was legitimate, but now that the war is over the promises made are going to be kept; that while the minister, maybe through an oversight on the part of his officials, had failed to include in the estimates any reference to these projects, he at least would take the matter up with the Department of Reconstruction, because' Public Works is the department which will do that work, although Reconstruction may have to provide the funds. I should like at least an assurance from someone that as soon as they can get around to it the promises made during the war period with respect to these two particular projects will be carried out.

Mr. Chairman, I would not impute any motives to an hon. member speaking in the committee. The hon.
member who has just taken his seat is speaking of post-war public works, and I have explained that these estimates do not contain any post-war items. We just admit that. These estimates were prepared for March 31, 1945, to March 31, 1946. We were here presenting these estimates last spring while the war was on, and five-twelfths of the amount was voted at that time. Now we are just completing the fiscal year.* This does not comprise the post-war projects or works which we have, or which the hon. member has, in mind.
But fisheries won't wait for estimates.

The policy we followed of not proceeding in war time with extended public works projects was admitted by everybody, even by the hon. member. My estimates would not have passed this house if there had been an increase in them during the war. Everybody understood that we were in the war and were putting everything into it and that the ordinary public services had to wait until after the war.
As to the suggestion that a promise was made, if the hon. member will look up the estimates for the fiscal years 1943-44 and 1944-45 he will find there was no promise by the Minister of Public Works. The estimates went through in about twenty minutes each time; I did not even have to discuss them; they were unanimously agreed to, I believe, because the policy was the right one. My difficulty to-day is that I am getting into that period which is post-war, yet I am dealing wdth the ordinary civil estimates. If the hon. member has been patient so long on behalf of Glace Bay and Port Morien, he may be patient a little longer. He has been waiting, he says, ten years for those works, and I have been here only three, so I can take only three-tenths of the blame.

The problem is becoming
worse every year. .
I could ask perhaps fifty members in the house to stand up, and they would make the same speech the hon. member has made.
I am going to make one now.

I may have to make a speech that way, and I do not contradict what the hon. member has said. I may not agree with everything he has said, but I really do not think this is the right time to discuss post-war projects. I would
Supply-Public Works

not be prepared to discuss them in detail, because I have not the details here. I am ready to discuss every item of ordinary estimates, and I think it is only fair to my officials to confine the discussion to those items. To assume that my officials were negligent would not, I suggest, be a fair assumption.	.
I did not say that! I said there was an oversight.

Well, there was no oversight on the part of the officials of the Department of Public Works. They knew their position and they followed the policy handed down to them not only by the government but by, parliament of that time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has stated that these estimates do not include postwar estimates, and has made the suggestion that post-war projects should be considered when the items for another department are before the committee.
The Department of Reconstruction is in here too, but there is practically no vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Department of
Reconstruction will come up later, but it is not now before the committee. I would remind hon. members that we now have before us the estimates for the Department of Public Works, and -that those estimates do not include any post-war projects. Therefore I suggest that what is not intended by the estimates should not be discussed. However,
I am in the hands of the committee.

Surely we have the right to know now what the plans are with respect to public works being used as an adjunct to the general improvement of conditions, and the assurance that there will be jobs during the transition period' through which we are now passing. Whefi this matter was discussed last year the minister pointed out, and quite properly, that we were in the midst of war. When reference was made to the white paper issued by the government, dealing with the question of employment after the war, the answer given at that time, and accepted by the opposition, was that then was not the time or the occasion to discuss post-war employment as applied to public works. I do not raise any objection to your ruling, sir, but I think it is only fair and proper to point out that now that the war is over-officially or otherwise-we should have from the government, through the Minister of Public Works, a statement outlining 
generally the plans of his department. When the Minister of Reconstruction is before us, and a matter of public works is raised, we receive the answer that the matter is one for the Minister of Public Works. When we now approach the Minister of Public Works to ascertain what he is going to do with reference to this matter, the implication we must draw from his remarks is that it should come under some other department.

No; I wish to correct the hon. member-not under another department. It will be under this department, when the next estimates are prepared. These are not new estimates; they were prepared during the war and are a continuation of the estimates, seven-twelfths of which were voted in April last, for the fiscal year from April, 1945, to the end of March, 1946.
The hon. member is asking for a simple statement as to post-war projects. I cannot say: Yes, we are going to build a post office in such and such a place or a breakwater in some other place. I would have to cover the whole Dominion of Canada. What I may say in my statement is that it is the intention of the government to keep in good repair- better than during the war years-all the public works in Canada, and to undertake post-war works which will be prepared in my department, but submitted' to the Department of Reconstruction, according to the conditions in the part of the country in which those projects will be executed. The remainder will be prepared in the Department of Public Works with the staff at our disposal. The Department of Reconstruction will draw up surveys of their own and will try to give us direction as to what works should be proceeded with at a specified time. I believe that is about all I can say.

I cannot accept the minister's explanation at all. Men are coming back from overseas; others are being discharged from industry. They are taking new jobs. One of the means whereby jobs will be assured, according to the plans of the government as outlined in white papers, and according to other documents issued with such abandon by some departments, will be in the initiation of public works and they must be commenced not after March, 1946, but now. Certainly plans must have been made by this time. Surely the Department of Public Works is in a position to place before the committee something of its plans.
I direct my attention to my own province of Saskatchewan, which is going to have a good deal of unemployment-let there be no mistake about that. Those who left Saskat-

Supply-Public Works
chewan during the war are beginning to come back. They will not all be absorbed on the farms. Already there is unemployment in some of the cities. One of the means of meeting the problem is a public works programme, not without regard to cost or to utility, a programme to operate in cooperation with private and government enterprise, so as to assure jobs rather^than a return to the dole. When I look at the estimates I find that the total amount to be expended in Saskatchewan is the sum of $40,000. If I am not right in that, I am sure the minister will correct me.

That is the
amount under the architects branch.

What else is there? I find items for dredging in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. There is not much dredging in Saskatchewan-certainly not of the kind covered by the Department of Public Works. Then there is an expenditure for telegraph and telephone, but that is merely the upkeep of existing utilities, it is not in the nature of a public work designed'to assure employment.
What about harbours and rivers, as shown at page 38 of the estimates?

That is the item upon which I intend to make some observations. If the Department of Public Works intends to operate in conjunction with the Department of Reconstruction and the Department of Labour in an effort to secure jobs for the unemployed, to develop public works that will be self-paying and of benefit to the areas in which they are established, this is one expenditure that very well might be made in the province of Saskatchewan.
Almost in the exact centre of Saskatchewan is Long lake or Last Mountain lake, the greatest natural reservoir that we have in the province. It is a fine fishing lake; last year there was exported from the catch from this lake between five and six hundred thousand pounds of fish; it is also a summer resort lake. But it is receding year by year. Whereas in 1904 it was one of the navigable lakes in the province, to-day it has diminished to such an extent that if something is not done, in twenty or twenty-five years this great reservoir will be dried up.	,
Between 1898 and 1904 the wheat being transported from central Saskatchewan into southern Saskatchewan and then on to the markets of Winnipeg passed over this lake on barges. The prairie farm rehabilitation vscheme is engaged in the digging of dugouts
and the maintenance of necessary reservoirs for water, but upon the Department of Public Works primarily rests the responsibility for the preservation of Saskatchewan's greatest natural reservoir. Looking over a return that was brought down I find that the Qu'Appelle river, which adjoins this lake and must necessarily be the means whereby it is preserved, passed into the hands of the dominion in 1898 because its waters had not been disposed of prior thereto. In 1938 the Department of Public Works purchased the dam facilities that were constructed at Craven on the northern rim of the Qu'Appelle river.
Unless something is done to raise the level of this lake-the best fishing lake in central Saskatchewan, a lake which comprises the greatest bird sanctuary in the province,-its very existence will be in danger. This lake is the most valuable water reservoir along the Qu'Appelle valley and something should be done to provide for tapping the reserve waters of the south Saskatchewan river in June and July of each year and diverting those waters down the Qu'Appelle into Long lake, thus raising the level of the lake.
There may be fifty members, as the minister has said, who are looking for post offices or other buildings, but I doubt if there is any place in the dominion where expenditure of money would give greater dividends in enjoyment, the preservation of an agricultural area and the conservation of bird life than, the utilization of the waters of the Saskatchewan by diversion through the Qu'Appelle valley. By doing this, not only will the lake be preserved but irrigation areas will be opened up along the river valley and jobs will be provided.
This is one of the few areas in Saskatchewan where irrigation has been used. A number of soldiers of the first war have already established themselves in small farm projects made possible by such irrigation work as has been done. I understand that the total project would cost some $2,000,000. I realize that that is a large amount, but its expenditure would provide jobs for the unemployed of our province; it would provide work over a considerable period of time-it will take some two years to complete the job-for farmers during their spare time. It would assure the preservation of this lake which is so necessary to the future of our province and the continuance of agriculture in the adjacent areas.
I ask the minister if this is not just the type of work that the post-war plans of the government actually comprehend. Is it not just the kind of public project that is being done in the United States? I look at the
Supply-Public Works

Washington Congressional reports containing the plans of the United States government for the building of public works that will be self-liquidating and pay dividends in happiness and enjoyment, and at the same time provide employment, and then I compare those plans with the plans of this government in November, 1945. If members are to carry out their responsibilities, now is the time to place before the minister projects within the competence of his department which will provide jobs for our unemployed. If we deal with all the subjects we have been dealing with in this parliament and do not assure jobs, we are building for the most terrible crash that hag ever taken place in this country. We are building for the separation of province and province, for disunion and for the setting of class against class.
I do not want to see the government building public works that cannot be justified, merely going through the form of entering upon some construction or initiating some work for no other reason than to provide jobs. The Department of Public Works should assure jobs by public works properly planned to the end that as far as possible they will be self-liquidating. Those jobs should use raw materials and labour to as large an extent as possible during the transition period through which we are passing and which may continue for some two years. The government should step in wherever necessary and construct public works which will assure employment.
I think it is the duty of the minister, and I say this with the greatest deference, to place before this house and the country at this time the plans of his. department. Surveys have been made. Everybody is making surveys. But parliament cannot find out what is in those surveys. I say to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman: Take parliament into your confidence and place before us generally your plans-not just generalities, not something ephemeral, not something that we cannot put our teeth into. Let us know your plans for each province or generally for each area, and let us in a spirit of cooperation try to work together with you to the end that we place before you proposals that we believe to be necessary in the national or provincial interest. On our part we shall do our best to assist the department in facing this problem, which I say without reserve has not been faced yet. We have white papers and papers of every other colour, but when we ask the government what it is going to do, each minister says: Go to the other minister, because that particular matter comes under rMr. Diefenbaker.]
him. The Minister of Public Works, I understand, is on the committee that deals with these matters. Let him tell us now what is being done and what the plans are, so that when we go back to our constituencies we can say: Well, there is a minister who was able to place his plans concretely before parliament. The minister laughs. But if he has not those plans, we are in for a very serious condition of affairs. If he has them, surely we have the right to know now what they are.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope that members of the committee did not misunderstand the remarks I made prior to the speech of the hon. member for Lake Centre. What the committee discusses on the item "departmental administration" is for the committee itself to decide. It has; however, been agreed that under the first item a general discussion is in order, and my suggestion was that each member would not propose some specific pub-' lie work required in his constituency because the minister in his remarks stated that there was no provision in these estimates for specific public works in the different constituencies. It was not my suggestion that there should not be a general discussion on the question of public works and what public works were best for the community, but I do think that hon. members should not at this time discuss specific public works in their own community, for the reason that the minister has not included them in these estimates and such appropriations could not be passed now. As I say, I am in the hands of the committee; I am not attempting to dictate to the committee what shall or shall not be discussed. But the minister did state that estimates for specific projects were not included and that they should not be discussed at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I feel inclined to agree with very many of the things which the hon. member for Lake Centre has said, and his dissertation on public works in Saskatchewan was most interesting. I believe there is something in what he said about that project for Long lake and the Qu'Appelle river. I have to repeat that there is nothing in these estimates for these works, but they are kept in mind. I am not telling the hon. member that some other minister is responsible. I have never said that since I have been sitting in this house. I take responsibility for everything that goes on in my department. But if hon. members followed my speech I am shre they will not find reason in it to justify the gloomy picture that the hon. member drew of conditions in the near future.

Supply-Public Works
Everything in this country does not depend on public works. If you look at the amount of my estimates you will find that they amount to $16 million. The hon. member is now proposing that we go into a two million dollar project, so I think it will be realized that the welfare of our country is not solely dependent on public works. They are a part of our national economy, and can be of help. But if anyone has in mind that the ills of our country can be cured by putting up public buildings or even self-liquidating projects such as the hon. member has mentioned, I must say that my experience has been' that it is not done that way. I have seen moneys voted by parliament in the last fifteen years for public works to cure unemployment; far be it from me to say that those projects were wrong at that time, but the results were not very good. This whole question has to be studied, keeping in mind labour conditions, the work of the Department of Reconstruction and private enterprise. We must try to do our share, oi course, and personally I am convinced that we shall have to study projects in every province.
The hon. member started out in light vein , and said that Saskatchewan was getting $40,000 for public works. I point out that maintenance and repairs of public works there come under the architects' branch; that is, the estimates for harbours, breakwaters, and so forth, and I am quite willing to consider any requests for such work. But surely there are very few harbours and rivers and ports in Saskatchewan. There are not many places there where we can build breakwaters, although there may be a few; but in that respect you cannot compare Saskatchewan with Nova Scotia.
I was not suggesting that. I said that they were navigable rivers under your authority.

I am not ready to go over the Navigable Waters Protection Act with the hon. member without having it here and making a study of it, but if roy recollection of the act is correct the only jurisdiction this department has over navigable rivers is to remove any impediment to navigation. That is the main jurisdiction we have. I understand that many of these matters are contained in the brief which the dominion government submitted to the provinces, and I hope that some understanding will be arrived1 at with the provinces.
Once more may I say that these estimates are war-time estimates, prepared when we were right in the war and presented to the
house in April last and voted to a large extent, and what I am trying to do to-day is to get authority to take care of the remaining four or five months of this fiscal year. I do not say that this is all the public works that we will have; there may be supplementary estimates. I am pleased that this discussion on public works has taken place, because we have. been the unknown department for so long and now we are getting prominence in the House of Commons.
Mr. BRACKEN; Don't let that lake out there go dry.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Is the minister aware of the fact that in my district there are eight towns and villages, every one of which fequires a public building?

I have requests for public works in every constituency in Canada. I do not know whether they are all justified. I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre that we- should not erect buildings just for the sake of building them. They must have some utility, and the cost must also be considered.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

I do not want to
press unnecessarily the request I made before recess, but I still feel 'that the minister owes the'committee an explanation in regard to the general plan to meet unemployment. He said this morning that he was not one of those who would have criticized a plan <for public works, at the time, but an experience of fifteen years in the house has taught him that public works are no cure for unemployment. At least that is the interpretation I placed on his words. I do not disagree with him in that regard, but public works are a necessary adjunct to any scheme to tide over the employment situation during difficult days.
I did not have the white paper on employment and income before me this morning. I find that it contains the plans of the government in this regard, set forth as generally though not particularized. On page 15 of the report presented in April, 1945, after setting out the various plans that the government has in mind for the encouragement of private investment after the war and the extension of consumer demand and the development of an expanding economy, it says:
Supply-Public Works

Accordingly as an appropriate policy for this period the dominion proposes to press ahead with the planning of its own deferred works and invites provinces and municipalities to do the same. In addition, the dominion government will give consideration to methods of stimulating provincial and municipal governments to carry out necessary surveys and draw the plans for useful public projects in. defined categories to be executed when they are needed, to stabilize employment, probably some time after the Japanese war is ended. Further, the dominion government proposes to press ahead as rapidly as possible with surveys, aerial and other mapping and explorations on the results of which a new and forward-looking agreed programme for the development and conservation of natural resources must be built.
I call attention to those words "forwardlooking agreed programme." They indicate that even in April last the government had a "forward-looking programme" agreed upon. The document goes on:
Then the dominion will undertake its own deferred projects in those localities in which the decline of war contracts or other circumstances have made available labour, which can be employed on such projects and for which the locality gives promise of _ permanent employment. The government will invite provincial and municipal governments to cooperate in following similar programmes.
When I brought the Last Mountain lake project to the attention of the minister I did so because it is recognized that if the undertaking in Saskatchewan is developed it will mean that a very considerable area will be available for irrigation. It will mean that this lake will be preserved for its fishing economy and as a bird sanctuary and also as a necessary reservoir for moisture. It is a project that will be worth while. I did not put it before the minister as the only project, there might be in Saskatchewan, but as one which should be in accord with what the government intends to do with a view to assuring employment. The minister is fully conversant with the general plan for assuring jobs; that plan was known to the government in April last, and the reason I am making these remarks is that we have heard so much about two jobs growing where one grew before. That is the statement of one of the ministers, translated into simple every-day language. I should like to hear of one of these post-war projects that will assure the growing of one job where none grew before, because Saskatchewan people are coming back from the coast and from overseas and already there is a lag in employment in that province.
From time to time the member for Davenport has brought other projects to the attention of the government, and this type of project combines in itself the very elements mentioned in the white paper as the proper
TMr. Diefenbaker.]
ones to be considered when the government is deciding upon a project for the prevention of surplus unemployment.
The minister does not need to go into details. I do not ask what amount of construction he will do in each province, because he cannot answer that. But what are the projects which the government will enter into so that it may, by these projects, cooperate with enterprise and assure the relief of any prospective unemployment? He says that my view of things in the next months or years is not the proper one, that I picture a doleful situation in employment. Well, all I know is that in the evidence given before the United States congress, one of the outstanding economic leaders there said that unless something is done in the setting' up immediately of public works in that country, there will be, I believe he said, four million unemployed within the next year. In this country we generally follow similar economic trends. If we are faced with a like problem, if it is found that private industry cannot secure jobs or assure jobs, then what are the government's plans for public works?
So long as all controls remain on private industry, so long as a price ceiling is maintained-and I am not arguing against it-in the face of higher cost of production which the .manufacturer or the industrialist must meet, private industry cannot develop or expand, because of the fear that there will be no compensation for the extra effort. Further, in the transitional period-and I am supported by the evidence given before the various committees of the United States congress-public works have a definite place. In the United States, if I understand the position correctly, several billion dollars of public works are about to be undertaken in order to assure that during this period of transition from war activities to peace industry the slack in employment will be taken up by public investment.	[DOT]

May r. ask the hon. member for Lake Centre this question: Is he now arguing on behalf of public enterprise, or public enterprise during the transition period, or more assistance to private enterprise? I cannot quite follow him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member for Lake Centre might like to answer the question, but I must remind the hon. member for Regina City that we are now discussing public works. I think the question would be out of order at this time.

Supply-Public Works
I should like to say a few words at this point. Does the minister want to answer?
It will take me only a few minutes. I am pleased that on so many points I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre. He seems to approve the white paper and the principles laid down in it.
Yes; it was copied from the British and United States investigations.

That puts us on the same floor, and we can discuss this matter of planning. Public works has jurisdiction in two or three spheres. The general plan is that we are to expand our works in every one of these fields-buildings, breakwaters and so on. We are going to try to come to some agreement with the provinces in the development of natural resources. I have not before me the proposals to the provinces, but we shall be interested in every work which can help private enterprise to continue on its same level, or on a reasonable level. Where I agree for the most part with the hon. member for Lake Centre is that he admits public works are not a cure for unemployment, they may be a help. In an economy where the national revenue is some nine billion dollars and we have a public works programme of fifty millions or a hundred millions, it would be only a drop in the bucket to boost the standard of living or give purchasing power to the population, Hon. members do not want me to go into details.
This morning the hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke of Glace Bay. I am coming back to that. During the lunch hour I found that in the 1946-47 estimates there is an item prepared for that, but that is a postwar project which has been considered. It is ready. But do not ask me to bring in those estimates which were prepared last January, and which are continuing estimates of wartime administration, post-war projects. I do not think that would be fair, and what I am now saying applies equally to all of Canada. We could discuss that for a day or two, but generally I would not be able to give much more information than I am giving right now, I shall certainly, however, answer any question hon. members wish to ask when any estimate is before the committee.

I know that the committee
wants to get along and finish up the estimates, but I am not going to apologize for one minute at this time for joining with the hon. member
for Lake Centre in the arguments he has made. I think perhaps the hon. member for Lake Centre has occupied the time of committee to-day to a greater advantage than he has at any other time since I came into the house. I have in mind, Mr. Chairman, the fact that I sat on the reconstruction committee for some two and a half years. The object of that committee was to find post-war employment. We called in representatives of industry and finance from one end of Canada to the other, and the provincial governments were called in to place before the committee the public works projects they had in mind in their respective provinces, so that the government might start immediately to plan for the post-war period. It was emphasized in that committee time and time again that in the transition from war to peace the greatest medium for taking the first shock of returning service personnel and war workers being laid off would be the public works projects that might immediately be put into operation in each province in order to create employment during the period of the re-tooling of industrial machines for other means of production.
During the two years that I sat on that committee I did not think I was wasting my time. I heard the provincial premiers laying out immediate post-war plans and indicating what they were prepared to do. As there was at that time an interdepartmental committee handling the problem for the federal government, I thought that each department of government that had to do with public works projects would have its plans ready. The fact of the matter is that the minister comes before the committee-I am not blaming him; I am criticizing government policy, or lack of government policy-and tells us that they have no programme ready.
We went to considerable expense in bringing people from one end of the country to the other to have those plans prepared. The excuse cannot be given that the government did not know and that they are still probing the problem. The problem was set out pretty well to that reconstruction committee. Evidently it never got beyond the committee stage.
The minister says there is no possible chance of solving the whole problem with public works projects. I will admit that; but I also want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that there is no other programme in the maritime provinces. There is no war industry there, and very few were created during the war-only about one per cent. Those that were created there folded up in the past several months. Industries that were in Nova Scotia
Supply-Public Works

for years were syphoned off immediately upon the cessation of hostilities, and a serious unemployment situation has developed in that province. That applies to the maritime provinces generally. It is worse than it was in 1939. If the only department of government that has some money to spend to create employment in the province says that nothing is to be done until the 1946-47 estimates are brought down, that is a simple and plain statement that so far as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are concerned there are no plans whatsoever for employment, and we are going back exactly to where we were in 1939.
I have talked to the Minister of Reconstruction about reconverting war industries there. He has no plans. I say to the Minister of Public Works that in the field of. public works there are many projects that could be got ready immediately. I mentioned two this morning. I picked them out because of their urgency, and also because I was led to believe that in the 1945-46 estimates there would be an appropriation for the purpose of doing something about the two specific matters I mentioned this morning. But from the broad general picture, as I see it now, the only hope we have in the maritime provinces is to get some public worjes projects started until such time as private enterprise, which has the machine of production in its hand at the present time, is prepared to make up its mind whether it is worth while investing money in the creation of industry in those provinces. We have no other hope., and we have not that hope now until 1946-47. In the meantime the two projects which I spoke about this morning are left untouched. Seven hundred boats go in and out of Glace Bay harbour during the fishing season. You could not get into it last year, and if it is left until next year the chances are you will not be able to do anything about it. The same situation applies to the [DOT] breakwater at Port Morien. The upkeep of the community depends upon it. I could give the minister a long list but I did not want to do that this morning. The hon. member for Lake Centre has insisted this afternoon that something should be done. If the minister is not prepared to tell us what the department has in mind in each province, can we not have it by way of supplementary estimates? I appreciate the fact that the present estimates were drafted months ago and that the money has been spent. That is quite all right. I am prepared to let these estimates go through without any further discussion if the minister will say: I am going to consult the Minister of Reconstruction and also that interdepartmental committee which is supfMr. Gillis.]
posed to be handling the recommendations of the reconstruction committee; I am going to find out what they are prepared to do in the way of getting urgent public works projects started across Canada as laid down by the various provincial ministers to that reconstruction committee, and, having selected half a dozen projects in each province, which means the creation of employment, I am ready to come in later this session with supplementary estimates and make a start on this rehabilitation of the country of which we have talked for five years. If the minister will do that, I do not wish to discuss this any further. I know he cannot do anything on the set-up he has before him now, but I insist that it is the obligation not only of the minister but of the whole government to tell us definitely, as a matter of public policy, what they are prepared to do in the immediate future with respect to getting these urgent public works projects started, in order to create employment in the transition period.

I have been listening for the last hour or two to this debate in respect to post-war public works, and, so far as I can see, we are mixed up a little bit on this matter; I am, anyway. I think we are asking the wrong minister these questions. About a year ago a reconstruction committee was set up. It went into a fairly extensive investigation as to post-war reconstruction and, partly as a result of its activities, a department of reconstruction was set up or is now in process of being set up. I never visualized the present Department of Public Works as being the department responsible for post-war reconstruction, although I agree that the minister should have something in- mind as to what his department is going to do next year or the year after.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat says that the minister should tell the committee now, for it is his responsibility to do this and do that and do the other in order to find employment. Now, when did it ever become the business or responsibility of the Department of Public Works to find employment for people? That is a question which I think we should continually put before hon. members of this house and the people of Canada. We do not build post offices because we want to give men work; we build post offices because we have no post offices. We do not build wharves for the purpose of creating employment; we build wharves because we need wharves. I say that the purpose of the government is not to find employment, but so to legislate that the people of this country shall have economic security at

Supply-Public Works
the very highest level that our productive capacity is able to provide. That is the purpose of government.
I can quite understand the minister saying it is no use to ask him what he is going to do next year or the following year, because I know how the department is handled; at least he can correct me if I am mistaken. Departmental officials gather around some table and get their heads together and say: What are we going to do next year? Well, the member for so and so wants a post office; he is a Liberal, we will put up a post office for him. And the member for so and so wants a post office; well, what party does he belong to? So eventually he winds up the work for the year, and that is his programme: so many post offices, so many wharves, so many other public works. Then he goes to the treasury board-and that is the nigger in the woodpile. He goes to them cap in hand, makes a humble obeisance to them, and says: Gentlemen, I want so much money this year to run my department. The members of the board take out their pencils and do a little figuring. Regarding themselves as the custodians of the people's money they scale the figures down, and the poor minister is left to get along with whatever the treasury board care to say he is to have. I should like to ask the minister a question along this line, and he can answer it later. I am afraid he will have to be very careful how he answers it, because it has to do with the relationship between his department, and the treasury board, and of course he will have to be very polite to the treasury board or they will scale him down a little more next year. I should like to ask him if my diagnosis of his procedure is correct.
The hon. member is all wrong.

I should like to ask him if a happy relationship exists between himself and the treasury board. I should like him to answer that, because when we are discussing grants of money for public works under this department we are just talking peanuts. I want to know whether the treasury board is not penny wise and pound foolish. Look at the measures on the order paper. Here is one, standing in the name of the Minister of Finance, which calls for an appropriation of $700,000,000. That is a lot of money. Another order requires an appropriation in the neighbourhood of $750,000,000. That, also, is a lot of money. It is to provide other countries with funds wherewith to buy what we have to sell. I can never figure that one out, but I may not discuss that subject on this measure.
It seems to me that when you ask for a few billions you are apt to get it, 'but if you ask for enough to put up a post office here or something else there, the board can figure in those terms, because they are at just about the level where they are able to do a little figuring.
Of course we in this corner of the house look at things rather differently. I am. glad we do, because, you know, money is worth nothing at all unless it is spent. Our Social Credit philosophy is one of spending, and that one has when he spends. I am willing to vote any appropriation for which the minister may ask. The only thing I ask when voting money is that he shall spend it without wasting it. That is all I am concerned about. And when treasury board or some other responsible persons find they are spending so much that they have to tax so much more, then I just hope that they will tax so much, and the people will holler and shout so loudly Canada will wake up to the fact that the present policy of government financing is strangling them. Those of us in this group can shout our heads off about government finance, but the government will move only when the people begin to learn that they are being strangled by this system of taxation and debt.
I should like to ask another question of somewhat lesser importance. What is the process followed in respect to the management of public buildings? It does not matter which one the minister may have in mind. Let us say a public building is on some corner or some back street. Is there a superintendent who looks after the building? If the minister replies that there is, then I am perfectly certain that the superintendents of some of our public buildings do not look after them very well. I have passed government buildings and have said to myself; Well, if that is a picture of government ownership. I want none of it. If private industry kept its buildings as some of our public buildings are kept, it would not be in business very long. It is about time the Minister of Veterans Affairs saw to it that the windows in the Daly building were cleaned. One of these days he will not be able to see out.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And the hon. member will not be able to see in.
Maybe they do not want anyone to look in.

There is no light in that
department at all.

Sometimes I have wondered if buildings like that have janitors.
Supply-Public Works

I have a further point. When the minister brings in estimates in which he includes amounts for repairs to certain buildings, what happens when buildings have to have repairs after the estimate has been passed? In private business, if a stairway breaks down the management will realize that in order to do business a new staircase must be put in and they will go ahead and do1 it. What is the process when that happens in a public building? Do they have to wait for a year until treasury board discovers that they need some new stairs?
They just step things up a little.

Do the superintendents
of these buildings have a sort of contingent fund to do this, that and- the other thing? Looking at some of the signs in these public buildings one is inclined to say: What boy in grade II printed that? I suppose the minister has no money to send out to have a little sign painted, so he has to ask some school boy to write signs in pen and ink. Words may be spelled wrong, the S's turned tlje wrong way, and all that kind of thing. Perhaps the minister would answer one or two of these questions.	-
The building in which we are housed is a very fine one, and spotlessly clean-except, of course, when I go into some of the member's rooms; that is a little different. But the hallways are spotlessly clean, and we like to bring visitors here so that they may see the building. I am quite certain, however that if someone from another country visited some of the offices in the east block-the Department of External Affairs, for instance-he would think the whole government was on the bread-line.
He would think they were in the morgue.

I think a good fire over in the east block would be a good thing for this country. It would clean the inside out and put a new inside in. That is the way I look at some of these things. I guess I have said enough.

Mr. Chairman, the discussion on my estimates started out on a high plane. Questions were asked about the general plan for public works all through the country; it was suggested we should try to find ways to relieve unemployment wherever it showed up, and I followed that discussion with keen interest. The only thought that came to my mind when hon. members were speaking about planning was this: Do they 
realize that planning for public works means that we have to make out a list' of specific projects extending from one ocean to the other? Now, I could probably give the committee some information as to projects for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and going on out to Vancouver-
And New Westminster.

Yes, and New Westminster. I could probably give information about projects for buildings, works and harbours, along the St. Lawrence and on the two coasts. That would be a general plan. But I can assure hon. members that every day we are studying and preparing those plans. The only question is as to the time at which a .discussion of such plans should properly take place. I shall not repeat what I said before, that these estimates were voted in part in the month of April, and I am now asking that a vote be passed to conclude the requirements for the fiscal year.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South has asked if we are to have supplementary estimates. Certainly we shall have a certain amount. But the timing of works is of great importance. If the department were asked to carry out some project in January or February along the coast of Nova Scotia, I do not think we could do it. We have to time our works properly. We start as early as possible in the spring and continue as late as possible in the fall. But the hon. member wants us to begin right away.
We have been waiting for ten years.
Oh, no.
It is time to get started.

Do not speak about the past ten years. In my department are officials' who have had experience in these matters, and who know the right time to go ahead with them. There are certain times in the year when some works cannot be carried out, and I hope the hon,. member will not insist that we begin next week on certain works in some parts of Canada. We have plans. The ordinary estimates will come up, and we shall have supplementary estimates at the end of this session. Then there will be estimates probably in February, during the next session. We shall have works in the different provinces. I cannot give stated amounts, because those amounts might be over or below what I have in mind.
This discussion was followed by the speech of the hon. member for Macleod, who has a sense of humour well known in the house. He

has told us of the way in which he believes the Department of Public Works votes money, and he says that if Mr. So-and-so is a Liberal member, he has a great chance to have public works in his riding. But if the hon. member will look up the estimates he will find that there is more money spent in constituencies represented by members of the opposition than in those represented by members on the government side of the house.
I agree with that.

My officials are not Liberals or members of the opposition; they are civil servants. I do not think the^ have any political affiliations. They are loyal to their minister, and they try to do their best for the people with the amount of money they have at their disposal.
I withdraw.
I thank you on behalf of my officials.
You are describing Alberta's method.

I will describe the set-up. Canada is divided into twelve districts. In each district there is a resident architect and a resident engineer. These men have their own staffs. They have full knowledge of the different public works in their district, their state of repair, the cost of maintenance, and so on. They make reports to headquarters in Ottawa. They advance every reason they can to get appropriations to repair, build or maintain public works. That is the ordinary procedure. As a general rule, members go to the resident engineer or the resident architect to present their plans. They then come to us and we decide. We generally follow the advice given by the architect or . engineer. If you know of one engineer or one architect from Halifax to Vancouver who is derelict in his duty, I should like to have his name. They are doing a wonderful job. They are considering every request that is made. They are technical men who act as my advisers.
We do not spend much money. I am thinking of what was spent during the war.
I can remember standing up in the house and asking for $100,000,000 for public works in Canada, but who was ready to support the Minister of Public Works on that occasion? Not one single member. We pared down our expenses to the bone, if you will pardon the expression, because requests for the war effort were so urgent and compulsory that we tried to forget our own lives here in Canada in order to try to save what we were fighting
for. That was the position of my department, and we continued in that way until the end of the war.
Under this new policy I am going to do my utmost to see that needed public works are constructed, not fancy public works that are not needed. I think that is the duty of the officials and of the minister. We are the custodians of the money. You may laugh at the treasury board, but I want to tell you that I have sat on that board. You ask if that board studies the expenditure of the people's money. Yes, they do, from one dollar up. Previously I did not know the procedure that was followed, but now I know it is the best guarantee you can have that the people's money will be properly spent. They do not spend money unless there is justification for the expenditure.
That does not always fit in with what we have in mind as to public works. We think that public works should be built when they help a community to expand its activities, when they help a private enterprise to expand its activities. I have in mind right now the construction of a wharf that was started at Westview on the British Columbia coast. Why did we do that during war time? We did it because an industry at Powell River was willing to spend between $13,000,000 and $14,000,000. We thought we should be ready to spend from $200,000 to $300,000 to help put up the wharf, to do some dredging, and so on.
When are you going to complete the, harbour there?

That may be coming, but I am not making any promises. I just want to tell hon. members what we have in mind, and we are going to follow that up to the limit. I should like to continue this discussion for days. I hope that after hearing this, hon. members will not be so ready to ridicule men who have been working for the government for years and doing the best they can under the circumstances.

That is not the way it is done. The Department of Reconstruction was set up to coordinate govern-

mental activities in the post-war period.
