We representatives of the people have come here in the belief that we would get information from our associates in Ottawa, particularly [DOT] from the ministers. Parliament has been in session since September 6, 1945, and the people of Canada want to know what is going to happen, not only in the years to come but in the days and weeks to come. They want some notice from the cabinet ministers as to what they may expect in the immediate future. Conditions in Canada to-day are not such that time can be wasted, particularly when ' you consider the money that is t<j) be spent by the minister's department on post-war projects.
Apparently the minister has not seen fit to give the people of Canada any idea of what they may expect from his department. In 1944 the minister acknowledged receipt of a letter urging improvements in Collingwood harbour. These improvements were necessary in order to reduce by $1.40 per ton the cost of coal to the consumer in the Collingwood vicinity. The minister's department is not working very closely with the Minister of Reconstruction, because the Minister of Reconstruction informed this house the other day that he believed there was sufficient work to keep the shipyards at Collingwood and other yards throughout Canada busy for about eighteen months. The Collingwood shipyards were asking that improvements 'be made to the harbour because it is not in fit condition to permit an extensive shipbuilding programme. The minister's two engineers last year drew this extensive plan for the harbour of Collingwood, and I have copies of a

great deal of correspondence-this is only one-tenth of it-between the minister and his engineers. I was warned by the defeated Liberal candidate in my riding not to mention this matter in the house; but on the 6th day of June, 1945-and it will be remembered that the federal election was on June 11-after that gentleman had been in power for eleven years, without ever mentioning to me up to that time improvements in our harbour, he did say, and it was well published in the newspapers, that approximately $4 million was to be spent on Collingwood har-hour-a small item of $4 million! The hon. member for Lake Centre asked for only $2 million, but the defeated Liberal candidate promised on June 6, 1945 that the dominion government would probably spend $4 million on that one trivial item in the town of Collingwood.
After the election I was told not to mention this matter or nothing would be spent. The matter would still have to be left in the hands of the defeated Liberal candidate, as this government was still in power. My answer to that was this. I am the representative of the people of Simcoe county, and if they need public works and I can prove it, I defy any government to withhold those public works from those people. I do not need anybody to intercede, and if anyone does, we will let the people of Canada decide whether everybody is to be treated alike by the government. I have confidence enough in the people of this country to believe that when public works are necessary for the general benefit of the people of Canada, wherever they may be required, the people will see to it that those works are carried out by this government. Until I find out differently, that is my opinion, and if I do find out differently, the people of Canada will know about it.
I cannot understand why the minister up to this late date has given no intimation regarding the expenditures that are to be made on public works when this particular work has been urged upon him repeatedly by our town and our board of trade, especially in view of the fact that the Liberal candidate in my constituency declared before the election that $4 million would be spent on this work. The people of Canada want to know, and they have a right to know, what is to be done. In my opinion it was not good judgment for the minister to get up here and say we cannot discuss anything but past expenditures.

I never said
such a thing.

Pardon me if I am
wrong, but I understood (he minister to

intimate that we should stick to the appropriations he is asking the committee to pass. The people of Canada want to know what the minister's plans are for the future, and they are entitled to know. The Minister of Public Works referred this afternoon to New Brunswick. I should like to take this opportunity to bring to his attention certain works that are necessary for the improvement of the facilities at the port of Saint John, New Brunswick. The port of Saint John is one of two ports facing on the Atlantic that remain open throughout the year. It plays an important part in the export business of Canada. The minister a few1 minutes ago said that he proposed to spend-money on public works where it is necessary to help communities, but I would point out to him that these expenditures are asked for not merely to help the community but to be of benefit to the dominion as a whole.
The port of Saint John has modern up-to-date facilities for handling freight. It has some of the best longshoremen in the world. But it requires further facilities. This matter has already been brought to the attention of the minister by the mayor and council of the city of Saint John and also by the Saint John board of trade. I do not propose to take up the time of the committee or the minister's time this afternoon by reading from that report, but there are two or three recommendations in it to which I would refer briefly.
One is in connection with passenger facilities at that port. We have, as I say, modem freight facilities, but we have no modern passenger facilities. Those facilities were destroyed by fire some years ago and have not been rebuilt. Customs and immigration sheds should be provided. The board of trade of the city of Saint John understood that plans for these sheds and buildings had been made some time ago, but they recently discovered that no plans had yet been made. I suggest to the minister that steps be taken to have the plans prepared immediately and the work undertaken as soon as possible.
I wish to refer also to a wharf on the east side of the harbour, known as the McLeod Pettingill wharf. Plans were made *prior to the war to rebuild this wharf but owing to the war coming on this construction was held up. I hope if it comes within his
jurisdiction that the minister will give attention to the rebuilding of that wharf now that the war is over.
Then there is a wharf at the head of the harbour known as the Long wharf. Recommendations have been made that it be reconstructed and I would ask that steps be taken to have that done at the earliest possible date. There are other facilities to which I could refer but these are the three most important; the others are contained in the statements that have been forwarded to the government by the board of trade and by the mayor and city council of the city of Saint John.
There is one other matter. It has not to do with the port of Saint John; it has to do with some of the fishing villages along the shore of the bay of Fundy in the county of Saint John. No repairs have been made since prior to the war to the wharves and breakwaters in some of these villages. The result has been that they have fallen into disrepair and in consequence the commercial fishermen who live in these villages and use these wharves and breakwaters are placed at a very serious disadvantage. I ask the minister to look into these needed repairs, particularly to the wharf or breakwater at a village called Chance Harbour. This matter, I believe, has already been brought to the attention of the minister. Recently I received a letter from one of the fishermen in that community advising me that, the breakwater being so far gone, they had found it necessary this autumn or early winter to make a temporary breakwater to protect their fishing boats. The wharf at Lomeville is also badly in need of rebuilding.
Since these matters were brought to the minister's attention I would point out that there has been a very bad storm in the bay of Fundy so that these wharves and breakwaters, which were in a bad state of repair, have now been damaged to a greater extent with the result that work is urgently needed on them at the earliest possible moment.
In addition to the wharves and breakwaters I have mentioned, work is needed in Dipper Harbour in St. John county. There is urgent need for dredging in that locality. There is a considerable lobster fishing business in that harbour.- The lobsters are brought in by boat and truck to Dipper Harbour and when they get there they are put in what the fishermen call cars, which are large crates that float in the w'a'ter inside the breakwater. What has happened is this. The harbour has started to fill up, and at low tide, instead of these large crates that contain the lobsters

floating, they rest on the bottom of the harbour, the top of the crate being exposed, with the result that some of the lobsters are killed. That of course is a great loss to the men engaged in this form of fishing. I hope the minister will give attention at the earliest possible moment to remedying that condition.
I have looked through the estimates in an attempt to find some vote under which one may discuss rentals for government offices, but I have not been able to find one.

My discussion may go to the point where I may challenge certain policies with respect to rentals and advocate government ownership of those buildings, and I want to be sure that I shall not be deprived of an opportunity.

I support the representations made by the member for St. John-Albert with regard to the eastern ports. He has made an exceptionally good case for the port of Saint John. I have already placed on record my views with regard to Halifax, and I will not take up further time in that connection. I concur in what the hon. gentleman has said about the fishermen. I do not look upon this as an expenditure, but rather as an investment on the part of the country. When I suggest that the Public Works department should favourably consider the requests made for needed breakwaters and wharyes in the fishing districts of the maritimes, I am urging what is'really an investment, because, unless the fishermen have these breakwaters, they are unable to do their work properly and to bring home the catch that adds to the wealth of the country.
The member for Calgary West the other evening drew, so to speak, a triangle of labour, capital and the public. In this matter I would point out that we have again a triangular situation involving production, export trade, public works and finance. These elements enter into the. picture. Unless you have production you cannot have new markets and it is necessary, if we are to have production, to give the fishermen needed protection in the form of breakwaters so that they can go out and fish and bring back their product, adequately protected against the hazards which they have to face. May I say to the Minister of Public Works that when requests come from the maritime provinces they are for needed works. We do not make requests otherwise, and I would ask him to give them his favourable con-
sideration. They should not be looked upon as unnecessary expenditures but rather as investments for the good of the country as a whole, and especially, of course, for our part of the dominion.

As this seems' to be rather a maritime field day, and as other provinces down east have spoken, I do not care to see Prince Edward Island left out in the cold. In going through the estimates before the house I was looking for a revote of a considerable amount for Charlottetown harbour improvements. This is not something new that is being brought to the attention of the minister, because Charlottetown harbour improvements have been promised for many years. A start was made on them in 1913 and nothing else was done until 1941 when a vote went through this house for 1250,000 to begin improvements there.	[DOT]
At one time we had a royal commission- it was appointed in 1926 under the chairmanship of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan-to look into harbour improvements and other matters connected with the maritime provinces. I will mention only the part of the inquiry that related to Charlottetown. The Duncan commission was appointed by a Liberal governs ment. It brought in a recommendation, No. 18, urging the absolute necessity, from the point of view of Prince Edward Island transportation, for certain harbour improvements. This had been neglected, but in 1941, as I have said, a vote went through this house of $250,000 which was supposedly to be used as a start on harbour improvements in the port of Charlottetown. Material was brought to Charlottetown-lumber, steel and machinery -and harbour improvements began. All of a sudden the construction company received the command to halt, and did it so quickly that some of the piles that were half driven were left there, I suppose, to show where work might start again at some future day. Then, as if by magic, all the materials disappeared. After tracing it we found that it had landed in one of the upper provinces of Canada to be used in war construction. We had no objection to their getting a wharf up there, but we do take objection to our part not being carried out.
What I want to say to the minister is that if this revote to take care of harbour improvements in Charlottetown is in the supplementary estimates-and I hope it is, because it has been definitely promised to us that it would be in the estimates of this year, if not in the estimates now tabled, then in the supplementary estimates-I shall feel much happier.

Supply-Public Works________
I wish to say a little more with reference to improvements to the Charlottetown harbour. Another thing we have been promised for the last forty years is a ferry service. Engineers have gone over it time and again. In 1913 a start was made to build a marine railway slip- it is sometimes called a dry dock, but we have called it a marine railway slip. In 1913 the Borden government purchased a site for it and did some work on it, but when the war [DOT] broke out in 1914 the whole thing was dropped. In later years we have been agitating for it, and it was promised by both parties in the last election that this would be a real project in the harbour improvement of our port on the island. What would that mean to us? To begin with it is part of the agreement under which we entered confederation. We were promised that we should have proper communication with the mainland. One thing essential to our transportation is to have a place in our province where we can repair our own ships instead of having to send them up to the St. Lawrence. One of our finest ships was lost on the way up there for improvements. If she could have been repaired and overhauled on the island we would not have lost the SB. Charlottetown.
When properly built this marine railway slip will employ at least three hundred men annually just to repair our own ships. These figures are taken from the blue-book which gives the expenditures that have been made annually on the repair of our ships over a period of years. Besides, there are all the local boats which could be repaired as well as the boats that we might get from outside points if we had a proper harbour. I bring this to the attention of the Minister of Public Works so that even if he has not his postwar programme all ready he must see that this one is in it. When we come to some other items in the estimates we shall couple with it one of the things that has been definitely promised by both political parties. Of course they always make promises before an election, but we are going to 'hold them to it this time. Besides this marine slip me are going to ask for the building of a new bridge across the North river which will be known as the Brighton bridge. This bridge will give us a definite road and highway over the shortest route from Charlottetown to Borden. This is a matter that I shall take up with the Minister of Reconstruction or the Minister of Transport.
With reference to the harbour improvements, I believe I am right when I say that a vote in the neighbourhood of a quarter of a million dollars was put through the house in 1940 for this purpose. I know that materials were, bought and construction companies 47696-169
employed to do the work. We were promised that it .was only a beginning, and that the harbour would be definitely improved' to carry out the recommendations of the Andrew Rae Duncan commission of 1926. Can the minister tell me whether it is in the estimates?

I am sorry, but I shall have to disappoint my hon. friend to a certain extent. That item will not be in the supplementary estimates of this year; but I am told that it is in the ordinary estimates for next year. I did not quite follow the hon. member with regard1 to Charlottetown harbour. I believe that money was voted in 1940.
Yes.

A contract was awarded, and then public works had their holiday during the war time. The contract was cancelled and the materials which were purchased were sent to Saint John and Sydney, I believe, to help works which we had there and which had become necessary on account of the war. But we have never lost sight of the improvement of Charlottetown harbour. I am glad to see that both parties on the island agree on this.
The work was really started.
It will be continued next year.
The minister can give us an assurance now that it will start next spring?
I am speaking for the department. I .have an estimate ready to be brought down for the improvements in Charlottetown harbour next season.

With regard to the vote for the improvements in this harbour, why should we lose out on it? Why do we have to wait? The money was voted. Why should the minister not be able to say to us that this work will go ahead next spring?
Time has lapsed. We could not use that money after the end of the fiscal year. We have to have a new vote for the next season.

The minister ably described how jealously the Department of Public Works guards public money, and how the whole of Canada is divided into twelve sections with an architect and engineer's office in each. Can he explain to the committee exactly how his department will coordinate with the Department of Reconstruction and Supply? In the bill setting up the department, the old Munitions and Supply Act was changed in order that the Minister of Reconstruction might be empowered to enter into construction contracts, and it then went on to define the various projects. When the bill was before the house the Minister of Reconstruction said he was not in the construction business, but neither,is the Minister of Public Works. I presume that both departments will let contracts. It would seem to me, from the description the minister gave a few minutes ago, that his department is in so good a position, with its engineers and architects experienced in the erection of public buildings- or "projects", as the Minister of Reconstruction calls them-that many of these projects which will be undertaken in the future could perhaps better be carried out in the Department of Public Works than through setting up a new department of reconstruction which, in turn, will require to have its architects and engineers in various parts of Canada if it is to do an efficient job, thus duplicating services which we already have, at considerable cost to the taxpayer.

I do not think that the Department of Reconstruction will have a staff which could be compared to the staff of the Department of Public Works. They may have a certain number of architects or engineers as their advisers. Bu.t Public Works has the set-up to study public works projects, prepare plans and specifications, ask for tenders, and, if the work is to be done at a comparatively small cost, call for local tenders.

I do not believe the Department of Reconstruction will have the same set-up as that of public works. Our projects of building and .other public works will be continued through our own organization.

I am not quarrelling with the work of the Department of Public Works, but here under reconstruction and supply we have set up a department which is empowered to enter into contracts for buildings, aerodromes, airports, dockyards, roads, defence fortifications, et cetera, and enterprises for industry or reconstruction.

May I interrupt the hon. gentleman? Nearly every project or work he has mentioned would not come under public works. There may be some that would, but the works he mentions do not. The building of aerodromes never came under my department. We have no jurisdiction in that field.

No, but this is a new department which is being set up, although in a small sense it is a carry-over of the old munitions and supply department. If our construction is to take place under this new department, contracts will be called for, and obviously the department must have its engineers and architects to see whether those contracts are properly designed to meet the' needs and to be economical in their operation. Inasmuch as the minister's department has been engaged in public works over the years, why cannot his department more efficiently and more economically carry on these proposed new construction enterprises, particularly as the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said that he hoped his department would liquidate itself within four or five years and he would find himself without a job? If temporary works of the kind are to be undertaken in order to create employment, why cannot that temporary job be put under Public Works rather than in a new department, at great cost to the public?

As I understand it, they have started to use our organization. That is so to the extent that we know about these works. Any extra work I would not know about, but I know they will use our architects and engineers in their projects; they have been doing so in the preliminary steps.

If I may caution the minister, Mr. Chairman, I think he will find that, perhaps because of the-personality who will be in charge of reconstruction and supply, gradually the power and the responsibility

Supply-Public Works
will gravitate to the new man and be taken away from the old. I do not know any reason why, if the Department of Public Works is efficiently administered by a capable minister to-day, that department should not do the building. I may cite, as an illustration of what I have in mind, the Department of Transport, which also was under one of the ministers and had under its jurisdiction the Trans-Canada Air Lines. But T.C.A, was retained by the present Minister of Munitions and Supply when he gave up the Department of Transport and was continued by him under munitions and supply, for reasons which he gave at the time-that there was a big job in the construction of aerodromes, et cetera; and while he is no longer constructing aerodromes he still maintains that organization. I suggest to the Minister of Public Works that he had better be on his guard or he will find the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply trenching on his preserves and taking his engineers and architects, or he will find that the Department of Public Works becoming a mere shell and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply doing the main work. The situation should perhaps be the reverse. The minister has already a good operating department capable of doing this work,- which, again, as the Minister of Reconstruction has said, will be temporary work under his department. That would obviate the necessity of a duplication of architects, engineers and the rest, and the work could be more efficiently and economically carried on.

I do not want to be persistent in this, but I think we have the right to ask the minister to give us some statement in regard to the plans of his department for the providing of employment by public works as ancillary to private enterprise, particularly during the period of transition. My information is that a committee of the cabinet has had before it in the last few months a general plan, that a survey has been made of the dominion, city by city, setting out what the prospective unemployment will be during the transition period. It would be improper for me to say that I have seen such a plan, but I know that one exists and that there has been worked out by the experts a division as between private enterprise and public projects in the solution of the prospective unemployment problem.
So far as we are concerned we know there are plans-plans, plans and plans-but when you ask the ministers where the jobs are going to be, there is not a job in sight. There are promises of jobs, but never a concrete example of the type of work which is to be 47696-169$
undertaken. I ask the minister whether he has not been consulted by, say, the Minister of Reconstruction nr by the Minister of Labour, and given some indication as to how many jobs his department through the construction of public works will be asked to provide. How many is private enterprise going to provide? What is the surplus which may not reasonably be expected to be provided with jobs? What kinds of the public works does the government intend to undertake- not two years from now but immediately; for, in the words of the white paper, these public works have been planned and are described as part of a forward-looking and agreed programme; They have been decided upon, but try as we will, it seems impossible to extract this information. I do not know why. There should not be anything secret about it. There is no need of hiding it away; it does not have to be put under lock and key. If there are plans, let us know what they are; what distribution of moneys is to be made; what provinces in general are to receive it; whether it is to be used in the development of water powers, irrigation projects or the erection of public buildings. These are things which the minister must have information about. The file, as I remember it, is a very large one. It represents the activities of a large number of experts over a long period of time. It is in the possession of the government, and the minister must have a copy. We do not ask him to go into any unnecessary detail; but can he not answer this one question: What is expected to be the degree of unemployment within one year? That has been anticipated. Statistics have been prepared estimating it. I believe with reasonable certitude that the number can be given in advance.

Would the hon. member give me his estimate? That would be helpful to the country.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER:	Well, now, after
all, mine is guess work. This is the product of the work of the experts in the ivory tower. They have been working at this and have made either plans and estimates. Surely it is not for me to do so. How can I contemplate whether there will be unemployment, and how much?
But the government has the record. It knows how many men will be reabsorbed in manufacturing, and what manufucturing concerns and industries are going to expand. It knows the anticipated number who will be unemployed. even though physically employable. Those are the people for whom public works projects are designed so as to assist in tiding over the transitional period.
Supply-Public Works

I have studied this report on employment and income. I have studied reports from the United States, the national planning board scheme and the British scheme. They all, with one accord, set forth their plans in generalities. The United States planning board has gone somewhat farther than that and has actually indicated the numbers that will be absorbed generally through improvement in export trade, by increase in private investment, by expansion in consumption demand, and by public investment in other various ways, whereby improvement may be secured and maintained.
I am not asking this in any critical sense or to embarrass the minister. But he is the minister in charge of the department which will be charged with a tremendous responsibility. The report indicates that public works will not solve unemployment. But public works properly applied and divided throughout the country as a whole can operate as a cushion during the period of transition, and can take up the lag when men are being transferred from war-time to peace-time industry, and when there is a lagging behind in peace-time industry.
I do not think I am unfair when I press this matter. We have not been able to secure this information. I am not asking anything unreasonable when I direct the minister's attention to the certainty that what he anticipates will actually occur. But we are asking him to place the committee in a position where it may know that the government has more than plans. If all the government has is some plans in white papers, and in the minds of some experts, and if there is nothing in the mind of the practical minister to translate such plans into action, then I say they are worthless. They are just plans, and not jobs.
What the people of Canada want is not plans, but the assurance of jobs based upon those plans. I am not going to press the matter further. If the minister says he does not know, then the answer is perfectly clear. He is the Minister of the Department of Public Works. If he does not know, then all I can say is that we must accept his answer, and it simply means that the public works plans are contained in white papers, but that as yet they.have not yet been translated into actualities or into plans which will culminate in the development of public expenditures.

I was considerably impressed by the statement of the hon. member for Lake Centre in the forenoon session. I believe he had some good proposals. I doubt very much, however, if most of the discussion we have had on this point is really in order.

I believe we shall have to accept the statement of the Minister of Public Works to the effect that these estimates were prepared prior to the beginning of the year and during a time w'hen the country was at war. He has said that they were prepared to meet a condition which prevailed when we were at war. I am not, however, absolving him altogether from the obligation to bring in supplementary estimates to deal with certain projects which were delayed during those years and which, now that the war is over, might be discussed appropriately. But I feel convinced that we are not dealing with the larger programme in the proper place.
We have set up a Department of Reconstruction. The white paper was issued by that department, and we should hold the Minister of Reconstruction responsible for the programme to be carried on in the period of transition. When that department is before us, and before parliament prorogues we should insist upon having some concrete proposals to meet a situation of unemployment we are now convinced1, and I think even the Minister of Reconstruction is convinced, we shall have in this country before spring. But I do not believe that this matter can be discussed properly at a time when we have before us the routine estimates for the Department of Public Works.

I cannot let the hon. member for Lake Centre build up a case based upon guesswork-those were the words he used-for the future. He has envisaged our country as one in which there will be a great deal of unemployment from one end to the other. When Tasked him to give his own estimate of unemployment for the next six months or a year he replied that that would be only guesswork. But on that guesswork he builds up a case in which he seeks to prove that the Department of Public Works should have one of those programmes or plans in which we would explain how we would take care of unemployment in the country.
If one follows my way of reasoning, then all the arguments he has made up to now have not been based upon facts. He turns to the minister and asks, "Does the minister know anything about this? If he does not know let him say so, and I shall sit down." Then, later on he will tell the minister, "You do not know what is going on, or what will take place." In French we have the expression: "La maniere la plus habile de prendre son homme;" or, translated: "That is the way you can hang anybody." One will make up a case, and will then say, "It is up to you, if you do not know."

Supply-Public Works
But I will tell the hon. member one thing I do know, as Minister of Public Works. .1 know what my powers are, and I know what the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works is. If the hon. member will turn to section 9 of the Public Works Act he will see that this department has power over certain dams, hydraulic works, the construction and repair of harbours-not including harbours coming under the national harbours board'- piers and works for improving the navigation of any water, and the vessels, dredges, scows, tools, implements and machinery for the. improvement of navigation.
If we take that as the power, then our plans are prepared for the next year to increase our activities to quite an extent. We will increase those activities where they will prove useful for the community in the improvement of business in each section and in order to relieve unemployment if it exists. That is the plan we have in public works, which is only a small part of the reconstruction plan or programme to try to maintain employment in the country and create as high a standard of living as possible.
If you read section 9 you will see exactly what powers and jurisdiction we have in public works. We are going to exercise all those powers and develop the works that are under our control. I have estimates amounting to about $16,000,000 in a budget of four billions and a half, and I-do not think hon. members should expect me to be able to give them all the information they want. I am ready to tell my story, and the other parts can be told by the other ministers. As a member of the government I can tell the hon. member for Lake Centre that we in our department are prepared to go ahead according to our jurisdiction and power; but we do not intend to spend money uselessly.

I gather that no expenditures are to be made for new works, but that expenditures will be made simply for the maintenance of works and so on. Would the minister explain the machinery? Suppose a small post office or a building for public services is desired in a community. Would that request go through the Post Office Department and then come to public works with their recommendation?

I may receive
a request from the Postmaster General that because of the revenue of an office the/con-struction of a post office would be justified. Then I would have the resident architect make a report on the situation. If it were
favourable, we would proceed with our plans and specifications. The same would apply to customs and excise.
The original request would go to the appropriate department?

Absolutely.
Public works does not go out and just put up buildings; we do not go around' trying to impose buildings on communities. The buildt-ing must be needed and justified by the revenue of the office. In many places the income from the office does not justify a capital expenditure.
There are two questions I should like to ask. First, does the minister's department initiate expenditures on public projects such as breakwaters? .
Yes.

That being so, I wish to make a few remarks but I shall be as brief as possible. I was told I was out of order this morning when I introduced a matter in reference to the port of Halifax having to do with the transfer of the Queen Elizabeth from the port of Halifax to the port of New York. I feel I am justified in bringing up this matter under this item.
The question was asked on the orders of the day and I understand that the Minister of National Defence is to make a statement, perhaps to-day.

I do not wish to hold up these estimates but I want to place the case of Halifax before the government in such a way that it will recognize our claim. It is not Halifax alone that is affected; this concerns our whole nation. We certainly do not want the Queen Elizabeth or any other ships carrying troops from England to a United States port when we have fine ports on the Atlantic coast, such as Halifax, Saint John and others. I think it is due to our men who went overseas to fight for the good name of Canada and in the interests of freedom throughout the world to have them brought back to Canadian ports when they are being returned. With all due respect to what the minister has to say, I think he should look into this matter from the point of view of his department.
I think the late Sir Samuel Cunard, the founder of the Cunard line, would turn in his grave if he read the statement which appeared in last evening's papers to the effect that Halifax was not a safe port for the Queen Elizabeth or any other ship. I have photographs here showing hundreds of ships that assembled in the port of Halifax during the war. I have here one showing the Queen
Supply-Public Works

Elizabeth sailing into thie harbour of Halifax under her own steam in what; would appear to be the safest possible manner. I have one showing the Queen Elizabeth at the pier in Halifax and it would appear to any one that she was as safe there as a bug in a rug.
There is misunderstanding somewhere. This is of importance not only to Halifax but to the whole dominion, and an investigation should be carried on as soon as possible. This is an opportune time to bring up this matter. If a breakwater is required, or if the present outer breakwater needs to be extended1 or increased in height, then it is up to the Department of Public Works to investigate and make the extensions, if needed. I asked the minister if these things were initiated by his department and he said they were. That is why I am now bringing this matter to his attention.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion because I believe I have accomplished my purpose in bringing this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works. I am glad to see the Minister of Transport in his seat because the national harbours board is under his jurisdiction. I hope that action will be taken so that in the future we shall have no such statements as appeared in the papers last evening.

I
should like to speak on a subject that is of importance and interest to every member of the house. We in this group have repeatedly brought to the attention of the government the survey that was made by the welfare council of Toronto, which found that the minimum wage on which one could keep an average family of five living decently and adequately was SI,757.60. Let us consider the salaries that are paid to men who are working in the government buildings at Ottawa. There is one foreman at $1,320; twelve foremen, part time, at $600; cleaners and helpers, nineteen at $1,140 and three at $1,020; twenty-eight part-time cleaners at $500. Many of them are married men with families, and most of them are ex-service men because I see a great number of them wearing buttons. How can they live and bring up a family on $1,200 a year? We complain about industry not paying decent wages, but the fact is that industry is taking a lead from the parliament of Canada. We in this house owe a debt of gratitude to the cleaners, foremen and janitors for their kindness and courtesy to us members, for they make life very much easier for all of us. I know cleaners who go to work in the early morning hours and work not just eight but sometimes ten hours, and occasionally twelve hours a day, with no extra pay. The only bonus they get is the cost of living bonus, which in all probability will be cancelled when P.C. 1003 goes. The only hope for these men is, I think, organization. I should like to see them in a trade union, and that is one of the questions I wish to ask the minister. Would these cleaners, foremen and janitors be allowed to enter a union?
And is the minister prepared to see that they are given decent rates of pay over and above what they are now getting?

No one more than I should like to see these cleaners, helpers and elevator men receive higher compensation, but my personal opinion is that I have nothing to do with fixing the salaries of these classes of workers, who come under the civil service commission. They are all classified, and any member who has attended the meetings of civil service committees knows how complicated are these classifications and salary rates. I would be most favourable to increasing everybody's purchasing power and raising his or her standard of living. I am really in sympathy with these workers, but I do not think I am the one who can raise the salaries of these civil servants. That is one more thing that does not come under my purview, although I sympathize with every one of these workers. I happen to live in a town of labouring people, many of whom are my friends. I have listened attentively and sympathetically to what the hon. member has said, but I do not think he is making his request in the right place, although I would favour any such move.
His second question was as to these workers joining a union?
These workers have the right to join unions?

I have no objection unless the government changes its policy, and I have always understood that it favoured unions among the labouring classes. If the hon. member lives in Ottawa for any length of time he will see that they have unions, not exactly in the sense of labour unions, but there are four or five different civil service associations. I cannot give the names.
They are more or less social organizations.

Yes, but they interview government authorities and the civil service commission with regard to better conditions, wages and so on. I am not an expert in these matters, but in the public works department where there are labouring men there is an association of prevailing rates people who come regularly to see me and chat over their wants, and in the department there is a constant study of conditions of work, increases in wages and so on. I often recommend increases to the labour department where there is a body that sanctions rates of wages, and when a report comes back with their approval I put it
Supply-Public Works

before the treasury board. In the last year there have been, I will not say increases, but readjustments in pay, because we are still living under a condition of stabilized prices and wages which perhaps would hinder large increases in any class.
The minister has put his finger on the spot when he refers to the treasury board. Probably the treasury board has more to do with this than the minister or the commission.
Before the hon. member came in I spoke of the treasury board.

The question I am
about to ask may have been put before; I do not know. One cannot be here all the time these long days. I understand, however, that the department has a list of desirable public works graded under letters A, B. C. D. and so on-projects that may be undertaken in the post-war period for the relief of unemployment.

That matter
has been brought up before.
I prefaced my remarks by saying that perhaps it had been discussed before. If so, I will not go into it again. As I say, one cannot be here all the time to listen to what goes on.
Is it possible for the minister to make representations to see that these workers get better wages and that their hours are reasonable in this building? Ten hours a day is too much.
The employees in the buildings, except the elevator operators who are under the supervision of public works, do not come under the department.
They are the ones I am talking about, and also the cleaners.
The cleaners in this building do not come under my department. They are under the Speaker.
Then we shall have to raise this question in connection with the House of - Commons staff. It should be brought up.

This morning when I shut my window in the Chateau Laurier I was surprised to see, although I should not have been surprised, seeing that I brought the matter up last year, that the window-sill,

instead of being white as it was last night, was absolutely black. The soot comes from the Daly building across the street. I understand that there is an oil furnace there. There must be one because I see a 1,000-gallon oil truck practically every other morning unloading at that building. I do not believe the oil-burner in that building functions as it should because no oil-burner that I have ever seen-and I have seen a great number of them-throws out clouds of smoke worse than any train in the country. How the Chateau Laurier management has stood this so long I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Stood what?

The soot and dirt from the Daly building oil-burner. If that oil-burner were checked by outside engineers from the manufacturers they would tell you that it could not throw out all that dirt as it is doing at the present time.

We have an engineer and fireman in the building. It is an old building and the installation is quite aged. I admit we are having trouble with it, but during the war years I have not seen my way clear to having a new installation, and I do not know whether in the future plans for the capital that building will be taken into consideration. It is more of an eyesore than anything else.

Could there not be installed a soot arrester on the stack? They have them on other buildings.
Another thing I noticed this morning-and I thought it was a waste of time and money -was the snow truck going down the street, probably miles away, to dump snow.
That is under the federal district commission.

As the hon. member for Macleod mentioned, the elevator in the west block quits at five or five-thirty o'clock in the afternoon. The other evening I was there about a quarter to six and I saw a cripple going down three flights of stairs. There should be another man there to relieve the elevator operator so that the hours can be extended, because while people are working in the building the elevators should be running. If a fire ever occurred there, there would have to be an elevator running.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
For the past year I have been pressing to have a new veterans building in the city of Ottawa. It is about our first necessity. I agree with much of what the hon. member has said, and I think it is one of the first obligations on the admini-

Supply-Public Works
stration to make plans for the construction of a real veterans administration building in Ottawa similar to the one in Washington.
For the last five years we have been hearing every year of someone breaking or spraining an ankle going down the walk on the east side toward the hotel.
All these lands are under the federal district.
All right; we will bring the matter up at the proper time.	.

With regard to housing, cannot something be done so that before we come back next summer and have to sit in this chamber in the heat, the place will be aired? In the second place, can we not have lights that are decent and that will not ruin our eyes?
And loudspeakers.
Yes, and loudspeakers too, so that we can hear what everyone says.
Every request will be taken into consideration.

I intended to bring up the question of lighting. Has the minister made any arrangements for improved lighting in the chamber? In the rows at the back here, if you hold up a pencil you will get six or eight shadows from it, and many members have had to go and see about their eyes and get glasses. For a new member to bring this matter up, when the lights have been used for such a long time, may sound peculiar, but this system is antiquated and something should be done about it.

Has the government
given any consideration to the question of converting a large number of the temporary buildings into permanent buildings so that they will accommodate a great number of departments which are using rented buildings? I think the Department of Public Works have rented somewhere in the neighbourhood of 105 to 110 different buildings throughout the city on which they paid in the year 1943-44 in excess of three quarters of a million dollars rent. I asked the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services what was contemplated with respect to the building on Elgin street. If I recall correctly, he said that it was being turned over to War Assets Corporation. I think that building could be made more permanent and could be used for a large number of different departments. Has the government any policy with respect to this matter?

Up to September there was such a lack of space in the city of Ottawa that instead of giving, say 125 square feet per employee it was brought down to seventy-five feet. We thought at one time after August 15, or September 1 that we would see the defence departments decrease the numbers of their employees. That has taken place to a certain extent, but they were replaced by new departments such as the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare, which are expanding departments, and we find to-day that we have not too much space for our offices.
As to the future policy of. the government with respect to the temporary buildings, I understand that they were 'built and would be useful for a certain number of years. They will be replaced, as time goes on in this scheme of a national capital, with other permanent public buildings. Did I understand that they were declared as surplus to the department?
It was my understanding that the navy had practically abandoned the building and would turn it over.

I am sure that the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare will be glad the moment they abandon it. They are crowded in. Some of the employees were in halls for a while; they could hardly do their work. I am now trying to get them a little more space. As regards hygienic' conditions, when you have people working in that limited space of seventy-five feet, there is far less comfort than if they had 125 feet. I do not see that we can dispense with those temporary buildings in the near future.

speechtext:
May I tell my hon.
friend that the greatest problem we have encountered in veterans affairs across Canada is lack of space. Instead of cutting down we shall increase substantially in the next eighteen months. We have been having stenog-

raphers and secretaries working in corridors for the last six months. That condition should not prevail among individuals who are looking after the men coming back from the war.

I am not criticizing veterans affairs, but it seems to me that there are other departments which should be cutting down at the present time, and the veterans affairs department should be moving into the space left vacant by some of those departments. The Department of Munitions and Supply are closing down, and the wartime prices and trade board will be cutting down in a short while.

I was glad to hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs talking about the maintenance of the health of the workers involved in the various departments. I can recognize that during the war years those departments, because of the war, did not want to spend any more money than they could avoid, but when it comes down to the health of the people involved and it gets serious then something should be done. There is a telegraph office in Hazelton. I am not speaking of Hazelton because Hazelton wants a new building, but the employees in that building are suffering. They have colds continually; snow blows under the doors and through the cracks around the windows; flies enter in the summer. The employees freeze when they are a few feet away from the stove and when they are right near the stove they roast; they have to keep it red hot. Nothing has been done. They have one little piece of bakelite for the top of a desk and that is all they have had in the last two or three years. They are very proud of it; they pat it every time they pass it. I should like to know if the minister plans, and when he plans, to put a new building there for those employees who have worked very hard for the war effort?

This must be a rented building we have in Hazelton. I could not give an answer offhand as to whether or not we contemplate putting up a new building there. I do not know whether we own that -building.

It may be a rented building; I am not certain.
Mr. FOURNIER (Hull); I shall look into the matter and try to give my hon. friend a satisfactory answer.

and the job was apparently left at that stage. How much was spent on it? What is the intention with regard to this unfinished building? When may we expect to get it completed?

I should like to know whether the people of Flin Flon can expect that in the near future the department will go ahead with the construction of a new post office there.
I will look at the file and see what can be done.

I would ask the minister to tell the committee the present position with regard to the plans for removing Ripple rock in Seymour narrows on the west coast. There is a war vote of $287,697.

Certain expenditures were incurred in 1943 prior to the instalment of operations by a different method of removing the rock. It is a long story and my hon. friend knows all about it. At the beginning of the war the war committee of the cabinet was asked by the United States admiralty to try to remove that rock so that ships could pass through the narrows without any danger. That was in 1941. We had a vote in the war appropriation and we undertook that work. We tried one method of blasting out the rock and then dredging so that we would have a depth of twenty-nine to thirty-one feet. After a year and a half of trying we had to build a scow and some special equipment to do the work. We tried to anchor the scow down and started the work, but with very little success; in fact, we did not succeed at all, and at one moment we decided to discontinue the operations. Later on we were told that by trying the cable

method of stabilizing that scow we could do some drilling and blast out the rock. We tried that method. We did not have the money in the war appropriation but it was allotted by the treasury board to the department and I am now asking that it be confirmed. We kept on drilling until the end of October of this year. We drilled a little over 100 holes at a depth of from five to six feet and we blasted seventy per cent of those holes at that level. We are now up against the difficulty of trying to find a way to dredge this blasted stuff away.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Last night the committee passed resolutions 2 and 3. Resolution 1 stood.. Is it the desire of the committee to proceed with 1 or 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. 4, please.
That all payments of superannuation or pension to former employees or their dependents in 1946 or subsequent taxation years be taxable income, provided that, where a former employee has not in the past been entitled to a deduction from income in respect of his contribution to ' an .approved fund or plan, only a proportionate part shall be taxable.
Will the minister explain what is meant by the word "proportionate"?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will read the explanation of resolutions 3 and 4; resolution 3 is passed but,the statement I have covers both. Resolutions 3 and 4 should be considered together since they both are closely related to the revision in tax treatment proposed for certain pension plans, and each is incomplete without the other. At the present time there are in the income tax law two alternative provisions governing taxation of approved pension funds and plans. Under one alternative, contributions made into the plan by employees are allowed up to a limit as deduction from income in the year of contribution and the pension received by the employee after his retirement is. taxed as income. Under the other alternative no deduction from income is allowed the employee in the year of his contribution, but the whole of his pension received after his retirement is free from income tax. The first alternative is of more general application than the second and applies automatically in the case of any pension plan that has been approved by the Minister of National Revenue. The second alternative applies in the case of a pension fund or plan administered by a separate trust or .corporation established for that purpose which has elected, under the right given by section 5 (1) (h) of the Income War Tax Act, to have the income from its investments exempt from income tax. It is _ the fact of election under 5 (1) (h) that carries with it the right to a tax-free pension on retirement. Such an election was only of significance in the case of a plan where there was a separate fund holding investments which
earned an annual income. The majority of pension plans now in force in Canada are written on a group basis with the government annuities branch or with insurance companies, in which case there is no distinguishable separate fund on which income is earned.
The effect of resolutions 3 and 4 will be to place all pension plans henceforth on a uniform basis. Resolution 3 will do away with the necessity for any plan to elect to have the income from those investments free of tax, since the income of all funds will henceforth be exempt.
Resolution 4 will place all pensioners on an equal basis also by providing that contributions to the funds will be allowed as a deduction from income in the year of contribution, and the pension will be taxable as income of the pensioner in the year of receipt. It will provide, however, that to the extent that a pensioner had accumulated) a right to a tax-free pension because of an election by the fund under section 5 (1) (h)a that right will be protected to the pensioner and his dependents in future years.
I cannot answer my hon. friend's question at the present time. The formula for apportionment, for fixing the proportionate part will be contained in the bill, and the officials have to discuss it with me before final approval is given to it. There has been a great deal of discussion as to the principle upon which that apportionment should take place and11 have to consider two different principles and select the one which I think is most appropriate.
Would that be the life expectancy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that has nothing to do with life expectancy.
It would to a certain extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: For the rest of their lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Now, then, this changes the law so that the pensions of all will be taxable; but with regard to those who have been paying taxes on their entire income it is obvious that the entire amount of their pen-

sion cannot be taxed because otherwise they would be subject to double taxation; therefore a proportionate amount can be taxed. May I go on with resolution 5 as they are all embodied together? It seems to me that in this provision which, on the whole, I would consider generous and more than helpful toward providing for one's old age through contributions both by the individual and by the employer, there is a discrimination against employees in very small companies or against individuals who do not belong to a company which sefes fit to set up an employee fund of this kind. They have no means of providing under the same generous terms as have individuals of a large company or an approved plan, and there have been a good many complaints-I am sure some of them have reached the ears of the minister-that the individual who works for a company which has not a plan, and who would like to provide for his old age,, cannot take $900 from his income and have it tax free and put it into a fund from which he will eventually derive an annuity which will be taxable. Therefore, if I am right in my assumption, and these people are right in their complaint about discrimination against them because the opportunity is not open to them, I would suggest that the government might consider under the annuity department some method whereby the individual who is not an employee of a large company could contribute under the same right and privileges as the individual is given when he comes under an approved plan. I make that sug-

gestion because undoubtedly at the present time there would seem to be a rather harsh discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know of any way whereby that could be met.

In place of the company or the great number of companies having a plan whereby the individual contributes under it, could not the government, under the annuities department, set up a plan whereby individuals could pay into it and receive the same treatment that those employees of individual companies receive? As it is, when a man has $900 taken from his wages and paid into a plan on which he pays no tax it is a great advantage to him over a man who cannot contribute to such a plan. It is obvious under these plans which are approved, does the minister not think? The employer can also contribute $900. Then, under the generous provisions of last year's budget they can contribute $900 each year for a number of previous years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the employee of that small company were to purchase an annuity, under this legislation that annuity would _ be largely free from tax; that is, the capital element is free.
Would the minister mind talking to us also? The hon. member for Rosedale is not the only one interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought he was the one principally interested, but if there is general interest in this matter I will certainly try to speak louder. The employee of the small company which does not set up a pension plan may buy a government annuity, and he will be taxed on a very small part of that annuity. I do not know whether that entirely eliminates the discrimination, but he has paid a tax before he began to get his money back. It is true he has not been able to deduct the purchase price of his annuity from his income, as the employee of a company with a pension plan can do, but the employee of a company which has a pension plan pays a tax on every bit of his pension when he begins to receive it.	In the case of the purchaser of an
annuity-and that is the only provision I know of for the employee of a small company which has not a pension plan-under these provisions he is largely free from tax on his annuity, what may be called his pension.
And these three resolutions will equalize those two kinds of people who purchase annuities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As far as that is possible. If the hon. gentleman has not read the report of the Ives commission I would recommend that he do so, because it is an able and interesting document which makes a valiant attempt to eliminate discrimination as between those receiving annuities, pension payments and so on. They are not taxed in the same way. The pension is all taxed; everyone's pension is completely taxed. In the case of a contractual annuity, it is largely untaxed. In the case of a person who buys an annuity, that purchase price comes out of taxed income; he pays taxes on it, so to speak, before he buys the annuity. In the case of the employee of the company, he deducts his contribution from his income for tax purposes. One gets the benefit at one end; the other gets it at the other end; but as far as it can be done, in the opinion of this commission the situation is rendered devoid of inequity.

I should like a little information about something I have not heard mentioned so far in this discussion. Take the case of a farmer who has worked until he is sixty years of age. Then he sells his farm, live stock and equipment, pays off the debts he has accumulated during his years of endeavour, and invests the balance in an annuity. Where does he get off? What tax will he have to pay if he receives an annuity of, say $100 a month?
Not very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the hon. member for Rosedale suggests, the answer is, not very much. He will pay income tax on the interest element, not on the capital element. As I was saying a while ago^ if you ask me to state the formula for determining the capital element I can do so only in a very simple case. Take a man, say at the age of sixty-five who bought an annuity for a lump sum. In that case I could pretty well tell what the capital element is; it is the purchase price of the annuity. If he has a life expectation of ten years my understanding of the formula-and I have to go over this before I bring in the bill so that I can speak with greater certainty-is that the purchase price will be spread over the ten years, and it will be considered that one-tenth of that purchase price each year will be capital, that the balance will be interest, and he will be taxed on that interest.

Then tell me if I have it straight. Iff a farmer pay9 $15,000 in a lump sum-this is just by way of illustration-in

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The first question asked was this:
If a person purchased an annuity before the 25th June, 1940, whereby he would receive an annuity commencing at age sixty-five, having regard to the amount paid prior to the. said date, can he, after the 25th June, 1940, pay a larger sum than originally contracted for and thereby receive a larger annuity at the commencement date and have the larger annuity exempt from tax?
The answer is: Under the amendment of 1940 the increased annuity, or enlargement of the annuity originally contracted for, would become subject to tax.	(
The second question is: If the holder of the annuity purchased it prior to the 25th June, 1940, and then subsequently to that date advanced the date of -maturity and paid the required amount, as demanded by the annuities branch, would the annuity received at the advanced date be subject to tax in whole or in part?
The answer to the second question is: The ruling of the Department of National Revenue is to preserve to the annuitant all rights that he had in respect of his pre-25th June, 1940 contract so far as it could be matured earlier without the payment of any additional sum, so that if the date of maturity were advanced and because an additional sum was paid the same amount of annual annuity would be paid as and from the earlier date, then the difference between the preserved pre-25th June, 1940 rights and the amount that he would receive as an annual annuity, arising out of the additional payment, would be subject to tax.
To state it in figures for clarity-if the pre-25th June, 1940 contract entitled him to $1,200 per annum commencing when he was sixty-five years of age, and payment were accelerated by five years, -and he was to receive thereby, without payment of further moneys, $900 per annum from age sixty, that annuity would be free of tax; but if, after June 25, 1940, he paid an additional sum of money which entitled him to $1,200 per annum from age sixty, then the difference between $900 and $1,200 would be annual taxable income to him for the rest of his life.

The minister has answered my observations. But this in my opinion is a distinct breach of contract. Section 5 (k) was the section in question, and I doubt very

much whether under the present legislation the exchequer court would uphold the ruling of the commissioner of taxation.
If the minister wishes to know it, I shall not let this matter go by easily, because I think that in 1940 the minister permitted a breach of good faith on the part of the dominion government when annuitants were not allowed to enlarge a contract under the right which had been most specifically promised to them by agents of the government. It was so stated in the literature of the Department of Labour issued in connection with the sale of these government annuities. The minister quarreled with my statement last night that there had been a breach of contract on the part of the dominion government; but in 1940, when the debate on the budget was up, I mentioned this cancellation of the option right. An option right is just as valuable as any other intangible right. I said at that time, as reported at page 1480 of Hansard of that year:
I am not holding a brief for any person who pays in a nominal sum 'in order to obtain a larger annuity later on-
It may have been an improvident contract on the part ' of the government, but if a person makes an improvident contract he has to live up to it under the law unless he happens to be a sovereign body, such as the government. I continued:
-but the fact is that government agents did tell these people that if they took out small contracts they had the right to increase them up to a maximum of $1,200.
There was never any question about that. I have checked and rechecked. Other hon. members will bear me out when I say that the right was given to the holders of these contracts, even though it might be for a nominal amount. At that time the minister said:
I admit that has been taken away.
He was admitting taking something away from a person.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not admit it now, whether I admitted it then or not. I apparently misunderstood the hon. gentleman at that time because the right to increase was never taken away.

The right to increase under the same favourable terms as those given. What was the use of increasing the contract if you had not the same terms? Of course you could increase it to $1,200 if you wanted' to, but not under the original terms that you were promised. You were told that

you could1 enlarge the contract under the same terms, and that right was taken away. Section 5 (k), which deals definitely with that, says:
Provided that such exemption shall not extend to that portion of the income which exceeds the amount of the annuity actually specified in the contract before the twenty-fifth day of June, 1940, where such excess amount arises by reason of any option or contractual right to enlarge the annuity income by the payment of additional sums or premiums, unless such additional sums or premiums have actually been paid before the said date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Parliament did not say in that section that they were taking away any option or contractual right, nor did they take away any option or contractual right. Moreover, they left untaxed all annuities that were bought or contracted to be 'bought before June 25, 1940.

You have given me another ruling which takes away a further right. Take a contract for $1,200 which was entered into before 1940. So much was paid in and the payments were kept up. It was to be a tax-free contract for $1,200, and now you say to the committee to-night-there is the amount designated as an enlargement to bring the entire contract to maturity-that it will be taxable. If the minister has ever taken the trouble to look at the application form for a government annuity he will find that they were sold somewhat on this basis; I am referring to the period prior to 1940. The agent would visit you and state, "You can take out a contract for any amount not exceeding $1,200; if you take it out for a smaller amount you may enlarge that contract at any time." It was definitely stated in the /annuity contract that the income derived from the contract is exempt from dominion government income tax. That is what was stated in the contract signed by the Minister of Labour.
The agent would approach you and would tell you, "If you will tput down some money on one of these contracts you will be able to pay it off at any time you please under any plan you like." There were certain restrictions as to the guaranteed type of annuity. But in 1940 the tax-free option was taken away. I do not raise that point particularly, because I realize that if a man took a contract after that date and paid out so much money, while it was a breach of a contract, we could not do very much about it.
But when you come and say to the person who has an annuity for the full $1,200 and wishes to make it immediate under the terms of the contract which has a Dominion of Canada seal on it, that that will foe an entirely different contract, you are committing a breach. In the old days it made very little difference

to the minister whether it was tax-free or taxable, because even a single person had1 an exemption of $1,200. If he had a tax-free annuity, that would' probably absorb the complete amount. But when taxes rose, then the Minister of Finance looked into these matters, and he thrust aside all rights of individuals who held these contracts and said that they would not be able to get what they were told in writing they would get. Now they must abide by his decision even though it greatly changes the nature of the original contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My case is just this: Every annuity that any one bought or agreed to buy before June 25, 1940, is free of income tax. That is my simple case. But annuities upon which a person got an option but which he did not care to take up, were taxed as from June 25, 1940. The taxing of them was no breach of contract or breach of faith on the part of this government. On the contrary, had we left the law so that option holders could exercise their options and have their annuities free of income tax while new purchasers would have to pay income tax on their annuities, we would have been committing unjustifiable discrimination.

There is no use in labouring the matter at too great length. I do not know whether the minister thoroughly understands me or not. If he were a holder of one of these contracts, as many citizens are, I think he would put an entirely different interpretation on it. I have given him the case of people who have taken out these contracts for $1,200 before 1940.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At what age?

Any age you like; sixty
years if you wish.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Sixty-five years was the

This was simply a savings deposit with the government with the right to take out a Dominion of Canada annuity. The very application stated that tffe applicant would be granted an annuity of a certain amount or such other annuity as his payments might purchase. There was nothing very definite in the contract. It made little difference whether you took out a $100 or a $1,200 contract. That is what the agent would tell you because you had the right to enlarge it if you wished. As I said before, even a person who took out the $1,200 maximum annuity in 1940 is now, by a ruling which I think is not valid in law, told that his contract is changed. It is not an enlargement of the
contract; he stipulated for the full amount of $1,200 and now he wants to pay that up. Some people will have paid a fair amount by means of annual instalments and now they might wish to pay up the balance on their contracts. But the government now comes in with a new ruling as to income tax. I can only say that if the government continues to advertise itself in this way as a breaker of contracts,
I am very sorry for the future of the finances of this country.

May I ask
one question which applies only to the last answer given by the minister? Perhaps I did not understand him correctly, but I thought he made some moral distinction between the breach of a contract in the nature of an option and the breach of a contract which had finished its stipulations and covered the whole terri- . tory. Did I understand the minister correctly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

You see no
moral difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I certainly see a moral
difference.

Let us assume that I have agreed to buy a piece of property from you for $10,000 and I have paid you $100 because that would be all I would have at the moment. I then obtain an option for one year. You can see no difference in some third party, in this case the government, coming in and making a stipulation with respect to that, even though I had paid you the whole $10,000 in cash? That is the legal view which I think is simple. So where is the distinction between the government breaching a contract by way of taxation and breaching a contract which had not been completed? I cannot find the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You cannot deal with these matters in the abstract. You are running from annuities to real estate and you are not specifying the kind of change that the government makes in the situation, so that I cannot argue from one to the other. But take the case of annuities that I put. I have said it a dozen times. It seems to me that there is a great difference between the government going in and taxing an annuity which a man has agreed to buy, has either paid for or agreed to take and pay for, and an annuity which he has never agreed to take at all. The government has agreed to enlarge his annuity later if he wishes to pay the money for it. But the government has never agreed not to tax the additional annuity that he takes later. The government has not agreed

to refrain from taxing that. The man is out nothing. He has not paid any money; he is not denied the opportunity of investing his money elsewhere, and surely it is limiting the powers of parliament unduly to say that if you change your system from non-taxation of annuities to taxation of annuities you can only tax annuities which are purchased after the date of the change and not annuities which were bought on option and taken out before the date was changed. I think there is a great difference.

May I
endeavour to make myself plainer. We will leave out real estate. Say that I have a contract of insurance, which comes perhaps a little closer to annuities than anything else. Suppose I have taken out a contract of insur

 ance with a company or with the government, for they are all in the same positron, and under that contract of insurance I also have, the option, as many insurance contracts have, permitting me in a given length of time to uccept certain advantages which are open to me by the contract of insurance. With respect, I do not see the difference. I would be very glad to be shown it, but at present I cannot see it. Perhaps-it is my fault; I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there is any implied term at all binding the government or parliament that taxation would not be imposed after a certain date.
