speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
If there is, it is time that we quit selling annuities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I consider that the government carried out its contract completely.

With respect,
I know the minister thinks so; but I was trying to find the parallel, if there may be one, and I think there is. The minister has not explained my difficulty. That may be my fault.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is worth while to carry this on, but will my hon. friend point out to me in what respect the government broke its contract? The goviMr. Ilsley.]
ernment agreed by these contracts that the person who bought the annuity would have the option of enlarging his annuity.

Am I wrong in saying that an option between two parties involves one of the parties doing certain things on certain terms? I always understood that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly. That is your insurance company case.
If my simple understanding of this is wrong I should like to know. The government signed a document and gave me the right to do certain things within a certain time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
That is a contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
I think we shall go that far together.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
Then when I find that you as the grantor of the option have, by way of taxation, disturbed those terms-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What terms?
The terms upon which I might increase my position, the option part of it, if you wish. Am I quite wrong in assuming that to be the fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The act does not prevent anybody from enlarging his annuity. That was the only contractual term that is applicable.

I think we should get this untangled because it is very important. Is it not a fact that when I ptit $100 into a government annuity at a certain date it is estimated that that $100 by maturity will have earned a certain annuity,* and every multiple of $100 that I put in is a separate deposit which earns a separate part of an annuity which may total $1,200, let us say, at the end of a given time? In other words, I am not making a deposit which is in the nature of an option to do something at some future date. But I can put in another $100, or $50, or $500, or $1,000 when I have it, and from the date on which I deposit these further sums that money will give me at the age of sixty, we will say, an annuity of $500, $600, $1,000, $1,200, as the case may be. In other words, is this not in reality a separate deposit, with the deposits being made not regularly, perhaps rather irregularly, so that at a certain time a certain annual sum- will be available to me as earnings from that deposit? Are these not separate transactions? That is the point that was running through my mind when the argument was taking place, namely', that I am not buying an option but making a deposit which will guarantee me a certain return called an annuity, and my aggregate deposits may earn me, let us say, $1,200 when I have reached the age of sixty or sixty-five, as the case may be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the ordinary case of purchasing an annuity. The purchase price is not paid all at once. In most cases it is paid by instalments. But that is not the case I am talking about. I am talking about the purchaser who perhaps paid the government one dollar in 1930.
Yes, but the minister has not got my point. If I put in one dollar in 1930 that dollar in 1960 will have earned me very little.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

Perhaps I do not put anything more in until 1940 and then I put in $10,000. That $10,000 will earn me something up to the time of maturity. But as I see it, the dollar I put in did not entitle rae to a return of any particular sum other than on the dollar I put in 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
If in the meantime I make a deposit under different conditions, then I have to abide by the conditions imposed at the time I make the deposit. That is the point. Is that not the argument?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I can understand that, but I cannot understand the argument put forward by the hon. member for Rosedale, that you are buying an option, because it is a different thing from real estate, which was used as an analogy. I buy an option on real estate for one year and if I do not take it up at the end of the year I lose the deposit; but in this case I preserve my deposit and get an annuity on the deposit, and no more, until I make another deposit on which I earn something.
Do I understand that one has the privilege of increasing the annuity according to contract, but increases it subject to the taxation conditions imposed at the time the increase is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
That is perfectly reasonable and it seems to me to make good sense, but I cannot understand the argument advanced from the Conservative benches. It does not make sense.

If I can still throw some light on this matter I will try to do so, because what the minister has said does not budge me one iota from my position which I believe to be fundamentally right. If anyone in business attempted to do what the minister suggests can be done I would not negotiate with him at all because it would not be worth while. We cannot live in such a world. Let me read to the committee from one of these application forms for the purchase of a deferred annuity. This is _ one I found on my desk this morning. I do not think there is any marked change from those used some years ago. I quote:
I desire to purchase under plan . . .
One or 2.
. . . and agree to pay the authorized monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, yearly or single premium
Of so many dollars.
. . . reserving, however, the right to complete the purchase under the contract by the payment of sums of varying amounts . . .
Put in what you like, when you like.
... or by such other method as may be authorized and approved by the government-

-and with the understanding that such an annuity will in any event be granted to the annuitant as the total purchase money with interest thereon at 4 per cent per annum, compounded yearly, will purchase at the rates in effect at the date of this application, the annuity not to exceed $1,200.

[Mr. Jackman.1

If the other group have

I have no particular
disagreement with this resolution, except that I could not allow it to pass without commenting upon the importation into our whole tax system of a principle to which we have not given cognizance before either here or in Great Britain, namely, the taxation of capital profits. 16.	That the right of a corporation whose principal business is the production, refining, or marketing of petroleum- or petroleum products to deduct 40 per centum of the exploration costs and drilling'costs of oil wells which prove to be unproductive be extended to wells spudded in before the thirty-first day of December, 1946.

How is the productivity of wells determined? I have seen accounts of wells that had been capped, and no one knew whether they had been producing oil or not. They were in the exploratory stage at one time and were then capped. Is that a means of getting by the payment of income tax, or is there a method of checking to see whether they are productive?

Would the minister take resolutions 16 to 20 inclusive, which cover the oil well situation, and let u*s know what differences there are in the present legislation and what is contemplated under this resolution? With respect, Mr. Chairman, I think, if that were done, we would really 47696-1711
know what we are talking about, and it would cover the question which the hon. member over here had in his mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no change as far as the oil industry is concerned. I think all these resolutions deal with oil and natural gas; it is just an extension of the present legislation.
We are dealing with resolution 20.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right; it is just an extension of the present legislation for a further period.

This resolution is of interest to those of us who live in Alberta, and it has prospective interest, I am sure, to my hon. friends from Saskatchewan. I am asking tfye minister to give further consideration to one aspect of the picture. May I also say that I came down to see him in a private capacity some years ago. By that I mean that I was acting for a number of people and my trip was 100 per cent unsuccessful. I appreciated his position and he explained it to me quite clearly. However, in our business we occasionally get paid whether we succeed or not. I enjoyed the trip to Ottawa because I had lunch with him at his desk. I know he drinks milk at noon. That is all I came, to know. The point I am trying to make is this: Lest members in this honourable body think this is a small show -I have mot. my file with me-I wish to give one figure. Turner Valley is on the decline. That was our oil field. To-day it is producing
800.000	barrels a month, and that is not milk; that is a good deal of oil and it is on the downgrade. They have received some assistance in what are known as deep-test wells
The present programme, which includes that in the province from which my hon. friena comes, is greatly extended and is covering the prairie region. It is true that wells drilled there cost much less than wells drilled in Turner valley where the wells go down to
10.000	and 12,000 feet. If you drill an oil well there for $200,000 or $250,000 you- are doing very well. Out on 'the prairie they can drill them for $30,000. I think that is to a depth of 3,000 feet, and probably that will include some production machinery. In other words, the cost increases as the depth increases. To those deep-test wells the minister has given consideration and I am not asking that it be altered in any way.
We have heard discussions in this house to the effect that coal is a national industry. I am sure that hon. members from Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba consider precious metals a national industry. The point I make
Income War Tax

. is this, that the search for oil is just as much, and in fact more, of a national industry to us than any of those others. Why? With 800,000 barrels a month at the present time vve have never produced enough oil in Canada even to supply the Winnipeg market. We have at all times had to import oil to take care of the demand there. The reason is, of course, that the horse-anddouggy days in farming are gone-not gone, but nearly gone, I hope. I am glad the hon. member for Lethbridge is not in his seat at the moment, or he would accuse me again of doing harm to some other western industry. What I have in mind is this: The world operates on oil; there is .no doubt about that. I am asking that the minister have some regard to these explorations which are going on, other than deep-test wells, in the prairie areas. Turner valley is in the foothills, the sub-mountainous area, if one might use that expression. *
What has happened is this. In western Canada to-day we have a search and an exploration going on which is new in the whole history of this country. Every United States company of any account or size is in there. They have seismograph and geophysical parties there. I am not sure' that I know what these words mean; they are big words and I like to use them. They are spending a tremendous amount of money on these parties. The reason they are doing so-and I got this from the president of one of the largest companies whom I saw only a few months ago- is that in the United States they have a ninety per cent exemption of income tax on explorations. Therefore, do not let us think in western Canada that they are attracted out there because they like us, or anything of that kind. They have a wonderful exemption over there.
Let no one think I am making a percentage comparison between Canada and the United States, because so many other elements enter into that calculation. While we have forty per cent exemption here and they have ninety per cent there, the figures do not mean just that. Somebody said that figures never lie, but there is always the converse of that proposition which I am sure it would be unparliamentary to mention. I am not suggesting that this is the comparison, but I am frankly admitting and saying that the tremendous exploration programme we have at the present time comes from that.
I am asking the minister that with respect bo this prairie development, which is an entirely different show, we have some write-off. The minister says that there is no change; I am 
accepting his word for that. Aside from the ordinary drawback of forty per cent and twenty-six and two-thirds per cent and whatever it is on the shallow wells, there is no special exemption for prairie wells as there is for deep-test wells. I merely ask that they be given further consideration, because we cannot get our coal down to the east on account of the freight rate of $8; but we can build pipelines and carry oil. That barrier will never exist between eastern and western Canada if we can develop oil in real quantity. You can build pipelines a lot cheaper than you can build railways, and once you have them built they do not cost as much to operate as railways do. I am merely asking the minister-and I see his most excellent adviser in front of him, who, I think, is Doctor Eaton, who has always been sympathetic to this thing-to have just a bit of regard, a good deal of regard, for that prairie element which permits the newcomer and smaller companies to try hard to get some oil. Remember that oil was never discovered in North America by the big companies. History shows that it was discovered by the little wild-catter, and that is the chap I am thinking of at the present time.
The big companies buy the small companies once they have discovered oil.

The hon. member is quite right. I have had a little experience in that regard. I made $2.50 myself by selling out to the Imperial Oil. They do absorb them, but remember from little things great things have grown. We have two or three companies out there now, the Anglo-Canadian, the Home, and so on, some of them just localized in Alberta, which have really amounted to something.
The hon. gentleman to my left, the hon. member for North York, is sitting here all atremble waiting to talk about mining. We are asking from the minister and those able people who advise him, nothing more than to be put on a level with mining. Down here some years ago-and I was here-exemptions were granted to new enterprises until so many years after they had mills in operation. Their business is the same as ours. If you put a hole in a beer barrel and let the beer run out, it will be all gone. Oil and gold are in exactly the same position; they are not renewable products. It is not like electricity, for instance, which comes from water power, or anything like that. Say I drill a well which costs me $200,000. I strike oil and I take out my $200,000, which I put into another hole. I have not made any money; I

Income War Tax
am just where I started, except that I have paid income tax on the product of the first well. In other words, my over-all position has not given me a profit.
I do not want the minister to think I am going so far as to suggest that we should be allowed to do that sort of thing indefinitely, because then no one would pay taxes. We would be merely building up reserves. Suddenly we would become a big outfit and perhaps would be rich before you found us out, though I know you are pretty good on a hot scent. My thought is that you might help us in regard to those people who are wild-catting, because it is nothing else in the prairie area. I know you have read in the newspapers that So-and-so has brought in a good well. Probably it kept going for four or five days and then salt water came in. There are so many difficulties and intrusions, with this, that and the other thing happening, that this is an extremely hazardous business. So, to conclude, before you bring down this legislation, would you please give some consideration to the problem we have on the prairies in connection with the oil business?

I think the minister passed over my question rather lightly. I asked whether or not there was any way for the Department of Finance, through its supervisors, to determine the productivity of these wells. I had intended to follow that up; and while the hon. member for Calgary West has ably presented the case for the development of oil, I wish to deal with the matter from another angle. I consider that the search for oil is important because oil is a natural resource and should be developed; and I feel disposed to say that the United States system of a ninety per cent deduction for exploratory costs is the right one.
Hear, hear.

Do not misunderstand me. On the other hand the Department of Finance could well get that money back by establishing a substantial royalty on the production of the oil that is found. My leading question this evening was, how does the Department of Finance determine whether or not these wells do produce? How do we know that these wells all through western Canada are or are not in production? I have seen a great many wells that have been drilled and capped. No one seems to know whether or not they ever struck oil. No doubt somebody knows, but certainly the general public does not know. Why are these oil companies holding back? It is obvious to me there is a reason. Is it because the deduction allowed
is not sufficient? Is it because of the threat of a royalty? There must be some reason. I suggest that we give a cutback of ninety per cent, let these oil companies go to work and explore, and then put a royalty on the production; and we will get the oil.
The dominion has no royalty; that is a matter for the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I understand the United States system, but I think they simply allow these exploration costs as deductible expense for tax purposes. If they have a ninety per cent excess profits tax and are in that category, then the amount they save in tax is ninety per cent of their exploration expense. It sounds better than it really is, because when taxes come down in the United States, as they will on January 1, 1946-
Yes, they are down substantially.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are down substantially, I believe to forty per cent. So that from January 1 they will get a forty per cent advantage instead of a ninety per cent advantage; they will get forty 'per cent of their exploration expenses off their tax bill instead of ninety per cent, which is the same as our provision under resolution 16.
I did not understand that was considered an excess profits tax. I thought that was a deduction from exploratory cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was the exploratory cost. The amount of the exploratory cost was deducted from their profits for tax purposes. If they were paying ninety per cent of those profits in taxes, then they -were able to deduct from their tax bill which they paid to the United States government ninety per cent of the exploration expense, but only by reason of the fact that they had a ninety per cent tax. When they have a forty per cent tax that ninety becomes forty.
Would the minister continue and tell me how they check on the productivity of these wells?
Perhaps I might ask the minister a question which will help my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to come back to that question later.

May I say the statement of the minister with respect to taxation in the United States and Canada is
Income War Tax

entirely accurate. That is why I said that when we spoke of forty per cent and they spoke of ninety per cent, they were not comparable figures. With respect to the other question the hon. gentleman asked, for a long time I have heard exactly what he has been saying, and I am one of those who thought [DOT] that was the situation. We heard of a big corporation who had gone into a place, drilled their wild-cat wells, made a discovery and then capped it because they did not want the oil to come on the market. Then, having capped their well and said it was a failure, they bought up all the ground around and had an oil field. I heard that story so often I almost believed it, but I made a number of investigations-[DOT]
You do not believe it now?
As far as I can find out there is not a word of truth in it anywhere.
Of course I will take your word for it.

You need not do that, because the answer is comparatively simple. When you have oil in a country such as ours, where you have a price that is profitable and where you cannot even begin to supply the present market, it is beyond reason that anyone should cap an oil well. I think my hon. friend is more interested in the gas sections, because in Saskatchewan they have not even obtained gas yet, except a little around Unity and a few places like that. Let me put it in this way: they do not supply anyone with it yet, because they have a bottle-neck they have not been able to overcome.
There is no doubt that the ninety per cent figure is quite right. I have gone into this matter with tax experts, some of them with companies right in the city of Calgary; and as far as the ninety per cent is concerned, if you figure what it is taken from and take our forty per cent and twenty per cent we are in a better position than they are. I am sorry to support the government, but that is the simple fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In regard to the matter of unproductivity or non-productivity, the test is . abandonment. The section of the act is section 8 (6), and the unproductive wells, forty per cent of which may be deducted from the tax, are wells which are abandoned within six months after completion of drilling. I do not think there would be any fraudulent advantage there.
Does the minister suggest that capping a well is abandoning it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Would the minister answer the question as to whether he would give consideration to this little prairie place of ours? Then, perhaps I might be of some assistance 'in connection with the abandonment of wells. I do not know what happens in the benighted province of Saskatchewan, where they do not know much about this business, but let me say that in Alberta we have an oil and gas commission, which is a provincial government show. However, the well must produce this log-and for those people who do not know what a log is, I will say it is the history as one goes down to the bottom of the well. It is not the same thing as hangs out from the tail end of a ship. No well can be abandoned without examination by experts who are engineers on that board. Further, no one can drill a well without having put up sufficient money in cash to pay for the abandonment, in the event of the Compaq' itself not abandoning the well, or not doing the work of abandonment. That means going out and shutting off the water, and so on. With great respect, let me say that the minister would have no difficulty in finding out whether a well has been properly abandoned, if he will remember that once wells are abandoned they are through, because the pipe is pulled in and there is nothing more except what used to be a hole in the ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the question raised by the hon. member for Calgary West with regard to the extension of this very generous tax privilege to companies which drill deep test wells-I mean the extension to a different type of well-I suppose I should not say that I will not give consideration to it. However, representations have been made, and I am somewhat reluctant to extend a privilege of that kind. In effect, the dominion government is paying half the cost of drilling those wells, and if they turn out to be good wells, the company, and not the government, owns them.
But (he dominion government gets the money back, do not worry about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It can be defended in times when the need for oil is great, but it cannot be defended forever, and I do not know whether an extension of the privilege could be defended at all. The reason for such a distinction between deep-test wells and other

Income War Tax
wells is, as I understand it, that the risk is very much greater-perhaps I should not say the risk; the expense is very much greater. You have to get an inYestor to put in a lot more money. Therefore there is some reason for saying, "We want oil. This is going to be a very expensive proposition. You will have to put up half the money-and that money will be a lot. Therefore we will put up the other half." But with a verj' much less expensive operation I do not think there is the same justification for the dominion government's putting up half the money. That is what it amounts to, stripped of its camouflage-and perhaps I should not use that word; I shall say, stripped of its other aspects.

The minister has enunciated a principle. A deep-test well is nothing more than a wild-cat. That is what it is. It is an effort to develop a new body of oil. Your first deep-test is going into the producing horizon, and going down to- well, I cannot remember those fancy names, but I believe it is called the Devonian, or something like that.
In other words, the principle is this-and it is a sound one-that the government has been prepared to assist those persons who are trying to develop new areas or new fields, whether they lie side by side or one above the other. That is what the expression "deep-test" means. That being the principle, I am utterly unable to understand the minister's position. Let us say that a deep-test will cost $300,000-and that is not unusual. I know the Imperial Oil company spent over a million dollars in one hole and they got nothing. So that when you get into this business you can very easily get rid of money, almost with the same facility that members of the House of Commons get rid of it when they are spending somebody else's money. The principle is the same.
It seems to me that the contribution should be made on the same basis, the whole purpose being to find new fields. Why make a distinction then, between an expensive process here, and an inexpensive one over there? I ask the minister to give that a little bit of consideration, because, remember, if we get a new' oil field, the money the government has exempted from taxation-and you never had it, you know-will be returned to you at least a thousand times; and if they could have counted up farther than that when the Bible was written I would have used that expression, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether I am expected to reply. I may say that I am not enthusiastic about this legislation-and
perhaps I am being too frank. I would be more enthusiastic if it had been more successful. I am willing to admit that private investors have put up a lot of money. I admit, too, that th^y have lost a lot of money. We, too, have put up and have lost a lot. As the hon. member says, we do not have it; but we certainly would have had it, had it not been for this provision.
You would have killed it, if you had not done that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, because the taxpayers to whom we gave these tax credits would otherwise have paid us a tax. They were all perfectly good.
Not all of them; most of them would have been broke.
How many wells in which the government undertook to pay half the cost turned out to be successful?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think one has been successful. There have been twelve or fourteen altogether.
Can the minister tell us what it has cost the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I can find that out.
I knew it about a month ago.
And the total number of feet drilled in those holes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that.

It would just be a
matter of multiplication.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall get that.
I could do it now.

As the representative of the constituency in which Turner valTey is situated, I should like to express the appreciation of the oil mem to the minister for extending this fifty per cent drawback in the case of deep-test wells. I know that a considerable number of the companies which have been engaged in drilling operations in the Turner valley are now hoping to undertake exploratory oil operations in the plains area. One of the things which will restrict their operations or in some cases probably prevent them is the fact that they will not get the fifty per cent drawback in regard to wells they may drill in the plains area. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary West, Turner valley has now passed its peak and will be a declining source of oil from now on. As far as oil production in Canada is concerned, it is
Incorhe War Tax

absolutely essential that new fields be discovered. Therefore the necessity for exploratory work is greater now than it has been in the past. I should merely like to support what the hon. member for Calgary West has said, and I think the' government would be making an extraordinarily good investment by extending this concession to wells drilled anywhere, whether they are deep or shallow wells. There is no doubt that if an oil field even approaching Turner valley in importance is discovered, the government will receive back a great deal more than they would have failed to collect because of this concession.

18.	That the right of a corporation, association, syndicate or exploration partnership, formed for the purpose of exploring and drilling for natural gas, to deduct 30 per centum of exploration and drilling expenses be extended to expenses incurred in 1946.

I should like to say a word about the production of natural gas in certain areas of Ontario. It happens that there is a natural gas field in the district from which I come. The production of natural gas is an important industry in that particular part of the province. Natural gas has primarily two uses. First, it is used to heat and light houses and, second, it is used by certain industries where heat is needed or for processing of one kind or another. A great many people have gas stoves and other types of equipment in their homes, and these cannot be converted to the use of any other type of fuel. Millions of dollars have been expended in equipping those homes, and it is essential that these people continue to get natural gas in the days to come. The development of the field and the maintenance of the supply is contingent upon drilling operations. These are shallow wells; they are not like the wells we have been talking about in Turner valley. The people who are interested in the production of gas cannot understand why a forty per cent deduction is made in the case of oil wells and only twenty-five per cent deduction in the case of gas wells. The need for drilling has become greater as time has gone on, but it has actually dropped off to a certain extent. These companies do not want to spend all their revenue in the drilling of wells and they are anxious indeed that some further provision should be made. Why is it not possible at this time to allow a deduction 
of forty per cent for the drilling of natural gas wells as well as for oil wells? This is a most important industry in the section from which I come. Cities like Hamilton, Brantford, St. Catharines, Welland and so on use gas in large amounts for heating purposes in homes and for processing of different kinds of new material. Why is it not possible at this time to increase the deduction to forty per cent just the same as for oil wells?
Mr. IiLSLEY: Because the depletion rate is twenty-five per cent in the case of natural gas; twenty-five per cent, of forty is ten, and ten taken from forty leaves thirty. That is probably Greek the way I have stated it, but that is what is done. If the hon. gentleman wants me to do it, I shall get a statement to show just why that is done. It is in the form of a tax credit, but the tax credit is arranged on the basis of the expenditure being a deduction .from income for income tax purposes. If you said that the expenditure was deductible from income for income tax and excess profits tax purposes, that would be one way of stating it, but you can state it in another way, in the form of tax credits. These tax credits are worked out in such a way as to be the equivalent of the rule or formula j I have just enunciated.
I wish the minister would look over the matter once more and see if some adjustment cannot be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No adjustment should be made because the two classes of company are being treated exactly the same. The expenditure is allowed as a deduction from income for taxation purposes on the assumption that none of the companies is in the excess profits tax class. If you have a company which is subject to the forty per cent corporation tax and you were, to allow the expenditures as a deduction from income for income tax and excess profits tax purposes you would get exactly the result that you would get by applying this formula. The reason they vaiy is that there are varying depletion rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I suggest that the minister look at the United1 States law, where 100 per cent is allowed for exploration purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, where there is a 100 per cent tax. They are allowed that as a deduction from their profits for tax purposes.

I realize the difference between ours and the United States system, but I think we should allow every dollar that is expended for exploration purposes irrespective of the percentage that it may be of profits or anything else, in the hope that some day we may discover an oilfield of major proportions in Canada, of sufficient proportions to compare with either the Oklahoma or the Texas field. But unless we are prepared to allow every dollar "spent in drilling as a deduction from taxation we are not going to encourage the development of the oil industry in Canada. I suggest to the Minister of Finance in all seriousness that its development is going to take a lot more money than is perhaps in the minds of many of us at the present time. It is not a cheap thing to do. It takes millions of dollars to bring in an oilfield. One well does not make an oilfield, any more than one swallow makes a summer. Unless we are prepared to spend and to encourage people to spend major sums of money we are not going to develop; we are not even going to find out whether we have a major oil Dome which some of the oil companies think we have in western Canada. I suggest that we let this resolution stand, Mr. Chairman, until to-morrow morning.
